References today: Godot Editor Tour · Scenes and Nodes · GDScript Basics · Movement and Input · Signals · Area2D · Spawning and Timers · Score and UI Use your checklist Pick up the Day 1 Student Checklist from your instructor. Check off each step as you complete it. If you fall behind, find where you are on the checklist and jump back in — you don't have to start over. The big idea A game in Godot is a tree of nodes. Each node does one small job — show a picture, detect a hit, play a sound. You snap them together into scenes, give them scripts, and the game runs. That's the whole engine. See Scenes and Nodes. Today we follow a tutorial step-by-step. Following first, inventing second. Tomorrow you'll change everything. Check off each step as you complete it. If you fall behind, find where you are on the checklist and jump back in — you don't have to start over. The big idea You already have a working game. A remix means: keep what works, change what's yours. Most of game development is changing numbers and rules in something that already runs — not writing from a blank page. A good first instinct: change one number, press Play, see what happened. That loop — tweak, run, observe — is how you'll learn the engine faster than any tutorial can teach you. b: ⬅️ Day 2 - Make It Yours · ➡️ Day 4 - Production Day Today you will: stop learning the engine and start making something original. By the end of the morning you will have a team, a locked one-sentence pitch, a paper prototype another team has already played, and a Godot project with a player moving on screen. References today: Tiny Game Design · The Tiny Game Rules · Constraint Cards · One-Sentence Pitch · Paper Prototyping · Team Roles · Sharing Files on a Team · Movement and Input Use your checklist Pick up the Day 3 Student Checklist from your instructor. You need all three exit-ticket items signed off before Open Studio. The big idea The hard part of a tiny game isn't code — it's choosing one small idea and refusing to make it bigger. A great tiny game does one thing and does it well. Today is about picking that one thing. Read Tiny Game Design and live by The Tiny Game Rules all week. INSERT IMAGE HERE The #1 mistake this week Picking an idea that's too big to finish by Friday. "Open world," "multiplayer," "story with cutscenes" — all too big. Take your idea and divide it by four. That's about the right size. Trust this. Schedule Block | ------------------------------------------------- | Design crash course — what makes a tiny game work | Brainstorm with constraint cards | ☕ Break | Form teams + pitch approval | Paper prototype + cross-team playtest | ☕ Break | Project setup + roles + player moving | Open Studio: keep building, or Day 2 micro-game | Design Crash Course Your instructor will walk through the three ingredients in every tiny game that works. Take notes — you'll need these today. The three ingredients 1. A clear player action. What is the one thing the player does? Dodge. Collect. Jump. Shoot. Avoid. Stack. If you need two sentences to describe what the player does, you have two games. 2. A tension. What makes the player care? A timer counting down, something chasing them, a score going up, a fragile thing they're protecting. Without tension, nothing matters. 3. A failure state. What ends the run? Getting hit, running out of time, dropping the thing, the meter filling up. The failure state turns the player action into a challenge. The formula Good tiny games are: [action] + [tension] + [failure state] Example: Dodge the Creeps = move + enemies keep coming + getting hit ends the run. Your turn: fill in the blanks for a game you love. Does it fit? See Tiny Game Design for more examples and The Tiny Game Rules for the constraints your game must meet. Design patterns to steal Pattern | Example | What the player does | Dodge | Dodge the Creeps | Move to avoid things | Collect | Pac-Man | Move to grab things before they get you | Stack | Tetris | Arrange things before they overflow | Race | Temple Run | Stay ahead of something chasing you | Protect | Missile Command | Intercept threats before they reach a target | Build | Grow | Make choices that change the rules over time | You can mix two patterns. But if you mix three, scope-check yourself. Brainstorm with Constraint Cards Work alone for this part — you'll form teams after break. 1. Draw one constraint card from the deck on your instructor's table. Read Constraint Cards to understand what yours means. Tape it to the corner of your notebook. 2. Your constraint is your creative limit. Use it. Set a 10-minute timer. 3. In your notebook, write down at least 5 game ideas that fit your constraint. Don't judge them yet — just generate. Bad ideas are part of the process. 4. When the timer ends, circle your top 2 ideas — the ones that excite you most. 5. For each of your top 2, fill in the formula from the crash course: - Player action: - Tension: - Failure state: 6. Pick your one favorite idea to pitch to teammates after break. Your constraint (one of these — or draw your own): One screen — the whole game fits on one screen with no scrolling One mechanic — the player really only does one thing One button — the entire game is played with a single key Idea not coming? Try these prompts - "What if Dodge the Creeps but you're collecting instead of dodging?" - "What if the player is the enemy?" - "What if the goal is to make the level harder, not easier?" - "What emotion do you want the player to feel?" ☕ Break Step away from your ideas. Your brain will keep working without you. Form Teams + Pitch Approval Form teams (10:10–10:20) Your instructor will help organize teams of 3–4 people. Here's how it works: 1. Each person takes 30 seconds to pitch their top idea to the room (or to a small group). 2. Your instructor will help you find the 3–4 ideas that are most buildable and most distinct from each other. 3. You then join the team building the idea that excites you most. Teams are formed around ideas, not just friend groups. Write your one-sentence pitch (10:20–10:35) With your team, fill in the blank: You are a who until . Examples: "You are a raccoon who stacks trash higher and higher until it topples." "You are a single firefly who must light 10 lanterns before dawn." "You are a blobfish who sinks deeper and deeper until you hit the floor." Rules for a good pitch: One sentence only. No "and also." A stranger could understand what the player does. It fits in 3 minutes of playtime. You can build it with what you learned Days 1–2: move, collide, pick up, score, timers. Read One-Sentence Pitch for more examples and what to avoid. Get instructor sign-off (10:35–10:40) Show your written pitch to your instructor. They'll ask two questions: 1. "Can you build this with two days of Godot?" 2. "What's the smallest version of this that's still fun?" Answer both. If approved, the instructor signs your index card. You cannot start Godot until the pitch is approved. If you get a "not yet," ask: "What should we cut?" Paper Prototype + Cross-Team Playtest Build the paper prototype (10:40–11:00) On blank paper (no Godot yet), draw your game: 1. Draw the play area — what does the screen look like? Where do things start? 2. Draw the player (as a shape) and any enemies, obstacles, or collectibles. 3. Write down the rules in plain English on a separate piece of paper: - What does the player control? - What kills the player / ends the run? - How do you win (or is survival the goal)? 4. Make a simple "turn sequence" — if you were playing this as a board game, what happens each round? Use index cards as "game pieces" Cut index cards into pieces for your player, enemies, and pickups. Physically move them around. It sounds silly — it works. See Paper Prototyping for what a good prototype looks like. Cross-team playtest (11:00–11:20) Swap your paper prototype with the team next to you. You are not allowed to explain it — hand it over and watch. The playing team: 1. Read the rules sheet. (1 min) 2. Play through the game using the paper pieces. (10 min) 3. Answer these questions on a sticky note for the building team: - "The moment I understood the game was when ." - "I got confused when ." - "One thing I'd add/change: ." The building team sits silently and watches. Write down what you observe — where did they hesitate? What did they misunderstand? That's your user research. ☕ Break Read your feedback. Talk to your team. Decide if anything in your design needs to change based on what you saw. Project Setup + Roles + Player Moving Assign team roles (11:30–11:35) Every person on your team gets a job. Write these on your index card: Role | Responsibilities | Producer | Runs stand-up, owns the MVP checklist, watches scope | Engineer | Owns the main Godot project file, writes core scripts | Artist / Sound | Makes or finds art assets, sets up AudioStreamPlayers | Playtest Lead | Runs each playtest session, collects feedback | On a small team (3 people), one person doubles up. Read Team Roles for details. Create the project (11:35–11:45) 1. The Engineer creates a new Godot project. Use your game's name as the folder name (no spaces — use underscores: ). 2. Before anyone writes code: decide how you'll share files. Read Sharing Files on a Team and pick one method now. Write it on your index card next to your roles. 3. Set up your project window size (Project Settings → Display → Window) — 480×720 is a safe default, but you can choose your own if your game calls for it. 4. Create your first scene: Scene → New Scene → add a plain as root → rename it → save as . Get the player moving (11:45–12:00) 5. Inside your Main scene, add a child → rename it . 6. The smallest version of your game that someone can actually play: they can start, they can win or lose, and they can restart. That's it. Everything else — extra levels, fancy art, particles — is polish, and polish is tomorrow. Write down every crash or softlock. Fix those first. Nothing else matters if the game crashes in front of an audience. 2. Title screen — does your game have one? It needs: Your game's name (big and readable) Your team members' names A "Press any key" or "Start" button that leads to the game See Scene Switching for how to load scenes on button press. 3. Restart works cleanly — after losing (or winning), can the player try again? Test the full loop: start → play → lose → restart → play again. Does it work every time? 4. A particle burst on death — a in your main scene, triggered from . Juice is last for a reason Juice can break your game if added quickly. If any of items 1–4 aren't solid, skip juice entirely. h: Common errors and what they actually mean
No error at all — it just doesn't work
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Foundations Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 4 - Production Day Your game will break. Every game breaks, every day, for every developer in the world. Debugging isn't the punishment for coding badly — it is coding. This note is where you come when something doesn't work. The one rule Read the error message. Godot almost always tells you what's wrong and which line it's on. Most of camp's "help me, it's broken" moments are solved by scrolling down and actually reading the red text. Where the debug window is Everything lives in the bottom panel of the editor (Godot Editor Tour). If you don't see it, press F5 to run your game — it opens automatically. You can also click the tab names along the very bottom of the window. Tab | What it shows | Output | Your messages, plus errors in red and warnings in yellow. This is the one you'll use 90% of the time. | Debugger | Detailed crash info: the error, the line number, and the stack trace (the path your code took to get there). | Debugger → Errors | A running list of every error and warning. Click one to jump to the code. | Debugger → Stack Trace | Shows which function called which function. Read it top to bottom. | Debugger → Misc / Monitors | Performance graphs — FPS, memory. Not needed at camp, but neat. | Turn on "Auto Switch to Remote Scene Tree" While the game is running, the Scene dock has a Remote button at the top. Click it and you see the live node tree of the running game — real positions, real values, updating in real time. This is the fastest way to answer "is my bullet even being created?" and "where did my player actually go?" Clear the Output before each run (the 🚫 icon in the Output panel). Otherwise old messages pile up and you'll chase a bug you already fixed. Print statements — your best tool writes a message to the Output panel. That's it. That's the whole feature, and it's the tool professional developers reach for first. What to print The goal is to answer one of three questions: 1. Did this code run at all? → Put inside the function. If nothing shows up, the function is never being called. That's your bug. 2. What is this value right now? → Label it! alone becomes a mystery number once you have five prints going. 3. How many times did this happen? → If you expected one bullet and Output shows ten lines, you found your problem. Print tricks Don't print inside forever runs 60 times a second, so you'll flood the Output with thousands of lines and the editor will crawl. Print there only while you're actively hunting something, then delete it. Clean up your prints before the Friday showcase. Leftover is funny until a judge sees it. Reading an error message A Godot error looks like this: Break it into three parts: — which file — which line (click the error to jump straight there) the rest — what went wrong Nine times out of ten the fix is on that exact line or the line right above it. Common errors and what they actually mean Code won't even run (parse errors) Error | What it means | Fix | | You wrote or and the next line isn't indented | Add one tab under it | | Typo, or you never made the variable | Check spelling; add at the top | | Mixed tabs and spaces | Delete the whitespace on that line, re-tab it | | Missing bracket or quote | Count your and , your and | Red squiggles before you press Play The Script editor underlines errors as you type and lists them at the bottom of the code window. Fix those first — the game won't even start with a parse error. The game runs, then crashes Error | What it means | Fix | | You're using a node that doesn't exist. means "nothing there." | Check your spelling — it must match the Scene dock exactly, capitals and all | | Same problem — Godot found nothing at that path | Renamed a node? Every in your script needs updating | | The path is wrong, or the node is a grandchild | Use for nested nodes, or drag the node into the script while holding Ctrl to insert the correct path | | Right function, wrong node type | only exists on CharacterBody2D — change the node type | | You added text to a number | Use — | | The file moved, was renamed, or never got imported | Drag the file from the FileSystem dock into the script to get the exact path | | A variable is empty | Assign the in the Inspector, or | No error at all — it just doesn't work These are the hard ones. No error message means Godot did exactly what you asked; you asked for the wrong thing. Symptom | Usual cause | Nothing happens when I press Play | You didn't save ( ), or you're running the wrong main scene | My changes don't show up | Same — save the scene and the script | Player doesn't move | Input action name doesn't match Project Settings, or the script isn't attached to the node | Player falls through the floor | Missing CollisionShape2D, or the shape exists but no shape resource is assigned (yellow ⚠ on the node) | Collision doesn't trigger | Layer/mask mismatch — see Collision Layers and Masks | Button/Area2D does nothing | The signal isn't connected. Check the Node dock → Signals tab for the green 🔌 icon. See Signals | Sprite is invisible | No texture assigned · node is hidden (👁 in Scene dock) · position is off-screen · it's behind something (z-index) | Timer never fires | is off and you never called , or is 0 | Enemy spawns once and never again | is checked on the Timer | Something happens 60 times instead of once | Your code is in instead of or a signal | Speed is wildly different on another computer | You forgot — see GDScript Basics | The yellow triangle A ⚠ next to a node in the Scene dock is Godot telling you the node is misconfigured before you even run. Hover it and read the message. It's usually "this CollisionShape2D has no shape." The thought process When something breaks, don't randomly change things. Work the loop: 1. Reproduce it. What exactly do you do to make it happen? "It breaks sometimes" is unfixable. "It breaks when I jump into the left wall" is fixable. 2. Read the error. File, line, message. Click it to jump there. 3. Guess out loud. Say what you think is happening: "I think the bullet is spawning but at position zero." A guess you can test beats staring at code. 4. Test the guess with one print. . You either confirm it or eliminate it. Both are progress. 5. Narrow it down. Cut the problem in half. Is the function even running? → yes. Is the value right when it enters? → yes. Is it right when it leaves? → no. Now you know exactly where to look. 6. Change ONE thing. Then run. If you change four things and it works, you don't know why, and it'll break again tomorrow. 7. When it works, understand why. If you can't explain the fix, you didn't fix it — you moved it. The 15-minute rule Stuck on the same bug for 15 minutes with no new information? Stop and ask. You're not failing — you've run out of things you can test alone. Bring your best guess with you: "I think the signal isn't connected, but I checked and it looks fine." That gets you a much faster answer than "it's broken." Rubber ducking Explain the broken code, out loud, line by line, to a teammate — or to a stuffed animal, or to the wall. Say what each line is supposed to do. You will very often catch the bug mid-sentence, before anyone answers you. This is a real technique with a silly name, and it works. Breakpoints (the fancy way) When prints aren't enough, click in the margin to the left of a line number in the Script editor. A red dot appears. Run the game — it will freeze the instant it reaches that line. While it's paused: The Debugger → Stack Trace panel shows every local variable and its current value. No prints needed. Step Into (F11) — run one line at a time Continue (F7) — resume until the next breakpoint Press Stop (F8) when you're done You can also write as a line in your code to do the same thing. Breakpoints are the grown-up version of . Try one on Day 4 when you're chasing something stubborn. Before you ask for help Run this checklist first. It resolves most bugs on its own: [ ] Did I save the scene and the script? ( ) [ ] Did I read the actual error text in the Output panel? [ ] Did I click the error to see which line? [ ] Is the script attached to the node I think it is? [ ] Do my paths match the Scene dock exactly — spelling and capitals? [ ] Is the signal connected (green 🔌 icon in the Node dock)? [ ] Are there any yellow ⚠ warnings on my nodes? [ ] Did I add a to confirm the code is even running? Then bring: what you expected, what actually happened, and what you already tried. Copy the error, search the error Pasting a Godot error into a search engine, minus your own file names, finds someone who hit the same thing. Every developer does this constantly. It's not cheating — it's the job.

h: Set your main scene (do this once)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Foundations Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot The Godot window has a few main areas. Learn these names — the rest of the week we'll say "drag it into the Scene dock" and you'll know where that is. The main areas Scene dock (top-left) — the node tree of the scene you're editing. This is your game's structure. See Scenes and Nodes. FileSystem dock (bottom-left) — every file in your project (images, sounds, scenes, scripts). Drag from here into your game. Viewport (center) — where you see and arrange your game. Tabs at the top switch between 2D, 3D, Script, and AssetLib. We live in 2D and Script. Inspector (right) — every property of the node you have selected: position, texture, speed, color. Click a node, edit it here. Bottom panel — Output (messages + errors), Debugger, Audio. When something breaks, errors show here. The buttons you'll use constantly ▶ Play (F5) — run the whole game (the main scene). 🎬 Play Current Scene (F6) — run just the scene you're editing. Great for testing one piece. ⏹ Stop (F8) — stop the running game. ➕ in the Scene dock — add a new node. Set your main scene (do this once) The first time you press Play, Godot asks which scene is the "main" one — the screen that shows when the game starts. Pick it. Change it later under Project → Project Settings → Application → Run → Main Scene. Saving Save scene: . Save before you press Play, every time. Each scene is its own file in the FileSystem dock. If the layout ever looks wrong Editor → Reset to default layout brings everything back. You didn't break anything.

h: How to do it in the editor
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Foundations Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot This is the most important idea in Godot. Get this and the rest is details. Nodes = LEGO bricks A node is one small building block that does one job: / — show a picture — detect when things overlap (see Area2D) — a thing that moves and bumps into walls — show text like a score (Score and UI) — wait, then do something (Spawning and Timers) — play a sound (AudioStreamPlayer) Scenes = a tree of nodes You snap nodes together into a tree (one parent, children underneath) to make a scene. The Day 1 Player scene looks like: For Day 3+ team games, a CharacterBody2D player is more typical: Children move with their parent. Move the Player and the sprite, hit-box, and hurtbox all come along. That's why the tree matters. Scenes inside scenes (instancing) A scene can be placed inside another scene — that's instancing. You build one Enemy scene, then spawn 50 copies ("instances") of it in the Main scene. Build once, reuse everywhere. This is how spawning works. Typical project: How to do it in the editor Add a node: select the parent, click ➕ in the Scene dock, pick the type. Make a node its own scene: right-click it → Save Branch as Scene. Now you can reuse it. Add a saved scene into another: click the chain/instance icon in the Scene dock, or drag the from FileSystem into the tree. Rule of thumb If you'll need more than one of something (enemies, coins, bullets), make it its own scene so you can spawn copies.

h: Connecting a signal in the editor (the easy way)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Foundations Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot A signal is how one node says "hey, something just happened!" and another node reacts. It's Godot's version of "when this, do that." Real examples: A fires its signal → spawn an enemy (Spawning and Timers) An fires → the player got hit (Area2D) A fires → start the game (Scene Switching) Connecting a signal in the editor (the easy way) 1. Select the node that sends the signal (e.g. a ). 2. In the Node dock (right side, next to Inspector), click the Signals tab. 3. Double-click the signal (e.g. ). 4. Pick the node whose script should react, click Connect. Godot writes an empty function in that script for you. Fill it in: The function name is just Godot's naming — you can keep it. Connecting a signal in code Sometimes you make a node while the game runs (like a spawned enemy) and must connect by code: Making your own signal Then anything connected to runs. This is how you keep score from a coin without tangling your code together. Mental model Signals are like a doorbell. The button (sender) doesn't know or care who answers — it just rings. Anyone connected hears it and responds.

h: Other things a tween can do
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Foundations Index The animation tool the rest of this reference assumes. Read it when you want anything to move, fade, pop, or slide. A tween animates a property from one value to another over time. shows up in six other notes in this reference — Collectables, Dash and Double Jump, Doors and Keys, Health and Lives, Juice and Game Feel, Moving Platforms — and this is the note that explains it. If you learn one optional thing this week, learn this. It is the single highest ratio of "looks impressive" to "lines of code" in Godot. The one-liner "Fade the sprite to invisible over half a second." That's a complete, working animation. Reading the syntax Part | Means | | make a new tween that runs on this node | | the node to animate — , , | | the property name as text: , , , | | where it should end up | | seconds | The form reaches inside a value: animates only the y, animates only the alpha (transparency). Very handy. Sequences: one after another Tweens are sequential by default — each step waits for the previous one. Three lines, and you have classic squash-and-stretch. Parallel: all at once Grow, fade, and float up simultaneously — the coin pickup effect from Collectables. Easing: where the personality lives The same movement feels completely different depending on the curve. Transition | Feels like | | robotic, constant speed (the default — usually the worst choice) | | gentle, natural. Good default for almost anything | | overshoots and settles back. Menus and pop-ins | | wobbles like jelly. Fun, easy to overuse | | bounces on landing | | very slow start, very fast finish. Dramatic | Ease | Means | | slow start, fast end | | fast start, slow end — most natural for UI | | slow at both ends | The two-word upgrade Add to any tween you already have. It will immediately look more professional. This is most of what "polish" means. Other things a tween can do That makes a score count up instead of snapping — a tiny touch players always notice. Looping The idle bob on a coin (Collectables): means "move by this much" instead of "move to this position." Waiting for one to finish Tween vs AnimationPlayer vs Timer Use | When | Tween | short, code-driven, one property, made on the fly — hit flashes, pop-ins, UI slides | AnimationPlayer | longer, hand-keyframed, many properties at once, editable by an artist — walk cycles, cutscenes | Timer | you don't want to animate anything, you just want to wait | Common problems Problem | Fix | "Property not found" error | The property name must be a string and spelled exactly: , not | Animation restarts and looks glitchy | You're creating a new tween every frame. Create it once, in a function you call once | Node errors after the tween ends | It got d mid-tween. before freeing, or use | Nothing happens | Tweens don't run on a node that isn't in the scene tree yet — don't tween inside | Two tweens fight over the same property | then before starting a new one |

b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 4 - Production Day How to make a character animate — walk cycles, idle bobs, flipping to face the direction of travel. This is the node the Day 1 player already uses; here's how to drive it yourself. Related nodes Sprite2D for a still image, AnimationPlayer for animating properties (position, rotation, fade) rather than frames. Setting it up 1. In your Player scene, add an AnimatedSprite2D child (or use the existing one). 2. Inspector → Sprite Frames → → New SpriteFrames, then click it. The SpriteFrames panel opens at the bottom. 3. In the panel, the animation list starts with one animation named . Double-click to rename it ( ), and use Add Animation (the paper icon) for more: , ... 4. Add frames to the selected animation: - Separate image files — drag the PNGs from the FileSystem dock into the frame strip. - One sprite sheet — click Add frames from Sprite Sheet (the grid icon), open the sheet, set how many columns/rows it has, then click the frames you want in order. 5. Per-animation settings, left of the frame strip: speed (FPS — 5–10 fits chunky pixel art) and loop (on for idle/walk, off for one-shots like attack or death). Test without running the game Select an animation and press the ▶ in the SpriteFrames panel — it previews right in the editor. Playing animations from code The script lives on the parent (the CharacterBody2D), reaching the sprite with : on an already-playing animation does nothing — safe to call every frame. The standard pattern: match animation to movement Add this at the end of , after : mirrors the sprite horizontally — draw art facing right, get left for free. ( exists for vertical.) The (not ) matters: when standing still ( ), the sprite keeps facing its last direction instead of snapping right. Exact-name gotcha: ≠ . Typos here fail silently or error at runtime — copy the name from the SpriteFrames panel. Platformer version (Platformer Physics) — air state wins over ground states: One-shot animations (attack, death) For non-looping animations, the signal (Signals) fires when the last frame ends: Without the , the node vanishes on frame 1 of its own death animation — a very common "my death animation doesn't play" ticket. Useful extras is a fun Juice and Game Feel trick: speed up the walk cycle when the player has a speed power-up. "My animation doesn't play" checklist (1) Name matches exactly (case-sensitive). h: What people actually build with it
AnimationTree — and why to skip it
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index The most artist-friendly node in Godot. Keyframe any property of any node on a timeline, with no code. Keyframe any property of any node on a timeline, with no code. Collectables, Hazards, and Moving Platforms all offer it as the no-code option — this is how it works. This is the most artist-friendly node in Godot. If your team has someone who thinks in pictures and timelines rather than code, hand them this note and a lot of your game gets built without them writing a line. What it can animate Nearly everything: , , , , , , a Label's , a CollisionShape2D's , an AudioStreamPlayer's playback. It can also call functions at a specific moment on the timeline. Setting one up 1. Add an AnimationPlayer node as a child of the thing you're animating. 2. The Animation panel opens at the bottom. Click Animation → New, name it ( , , ). 3. Set the duration (the number at the top right of the timeline, in seconds). 4. Select the node you want to animate, move the playhead to a time, change a property in the Inspector, and click the key icon next to that property. That's a keyframe. 5. Move the playhead, change the value, key it again. Godot fills in everything between. Turn on the auto-key button The key-shaped toggle in the Animation panel records a keyframe automatically whenever you change a property. It turns keyframing from four clicks into one. The two toggles you'll want Loop (the ↻ icon next to the animation name) — plays forever. Use for , , a bobbing coin. Autoplay on Load (the "A" icon) — starts by itself when the scene loads. Idle animations, ambient motion. Together they make ambient animation genuinely zero-code. Playing from code Wait for one to end: Or connect the signal in the editor. Call Method tracks (the powerful bit) An animation can call your functions at exact moments on the timeline. This is how you sync a sword's damage window to the frame where the blade is actually out — see Melee Attacks. 1. Add Track → Call Method Track, pick the node that owns the function. 2. Right-click on the timeline at the moment you want → Insert Key → choose the method. The designer tunes attack timing by dragging keyframes, not by editing timer values. That's a genuinely better workflow. There's also an Audio Track for playing a sound at an exact frame — footsteps landing on the right frame of a walk cycle. What people actually build with it A door swinging open (Doors and Keys) — rotation + a sound A moving platform (Moving Platforms) — key at each end, loop it A coin's idle bob (Collectables) — key , loop, autoplay A boss telegraph — wind-up, flash, attack, recover, all on one timeline A title screen intro — logo drops in, buttons slide up, all keyframed A death animation — sprite spins, fades, then a Call Method track fires A saw blade on a path — pairs with Path2D and PathFollow2D AnimationPlayer vs the alternatives Use | When | AnimatedSprite2D | flipping through sprite frames — a hand-drawn walk cycle | AnimationPlayer | moving/rotating/fading nodes on a timeline; many properties at once; artist-editable | Tweens | short, one-off, code-driven — a hit flash, a menu slide | They combine happily: an AnimationPlayer track can drive which animation an AnimatedSprite2D is playing. AnimationTree — and why to skip it Godot has an AnimationTree node for blending animations with state machines. It's powerful and it is not a five-day-camp tool — see State Machines. Plain calls are fine for everything you'll build this week. Common problems Problem | Fix | Animation plays once and freezes | Loop isn't enabled (the ↻ icon) | Nothing animates | You keyed a property on the wrong node — check which node each track targets | Animation fights your movement code | Both are setting . Pick one owner per property | Plays on load when you didn't want it | Autoplay is on | Snaps between keys instead of gliding | Track set to Discrete — set the update mode to Continuous | Movement looks stuttery | Animating a physics body's — use AnimatableBody2D (Moving Platforms) |

h: What people actually do with an Area2D
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 4 - Production Day The detector. An Area2D notices when something overlaps it and fires a signal — but it never blocks anything. Getting hit, collecting a coin, walking into lava, reaching the goal: all Area2D. Area2D is not a body This is the thing to understand first. Godot's physics bodies (CharacterBody2D, StaticBody2D and RigidBody2D) have physical presence — they stop things. An Area2D has awareness — it notices things and does nothing about it. | Blocks movement | Detects overlaps | Area2D | ❌ | ✅ | StaticBody2D | ✅ | ❌ | CharacterBody2D | ✅ | ❌ (by itself) | That's why the Day 1 Area2D player walks straight through walls (Obstacles fixes this), and why a CharacterBody2D player needs a child Area2D to notice it got hit. The setup An Area2D needs a CollisionShape2D child. Without one it detects nothing — this is the #1 mistake in the camp. The four signals Connect these in the Node dock (Signals): Signal | Fires when | | a PhysicsBody enters — the CharacterBody2D player, a RigidBody2D mob | | that body leaves | | another Area2D enters — a bullet, another hurtbox | | that area leaves | Body or area? Look at what's coming in. A CharacterBody2D player → . A bullet that's an Area2D → . If your signal never fires, this is the second thing to check (after the missing shape). Making sure it's the player Three ways, worst to best: Put the player in a group: select the Player node → Node dock → Groups tab → type → Add. Now every pickup, hazard, and trigger in the game can ask the same question, and it keeps working when someone renames things on Day 4. Better still, skip the check entirely by setting up Collision Layers and Masks so only the player can ever trigger it. Then the signal firing is the answer. What people actually do with an Area2D Pickups — coin, heart, key. Add points, then delete itself. Full build in Collectables: removes the node from the game. It's what makes a coin actually disappear. A hurtbox — a child Area2D whose only job is noticing damage, so the parent body can focus on moving. The core pattern of Collision Layers and Masks and Health and Lives: A hazard — lava, spikes, a bottomless pit. Doesn't block, just hurts (Hazards). A trigger zone — an invisible Area2D with no sprite. Walk in, and something happens: a door opens, a boss wakes up, a checkpoint saves, the level ends. A bullet — bullets are almost always Area2Ds. You want them to notice a hit, not physically shove the enemy across the room (Making Bullets). A screen-exit cleanup zone — or use , which does the same job with less setup. An enemy's aggro range — a big circle around the enemy. Player enters, the enemy starts chasing (Homing Enemies): Asking "who's in here right now?" Signals tell you the moment something enters. Sometimes you want to know the current state instead: This is how you make lava hurt every frame instead of only on the first touch. Turning one off Cleaner than disabling the CollisionShape2D and doesn't need . Other Area2D properties Priority — which area wins when several overlap. Gravity / Gravity Point — an Area2D can override gravity inside it. A gravity point makes a little planet that pulls RigidBody2Ds toward its center. Rarely needed, always a hit. Audio Bus Override — reverb inside a cave. Pure polish (AudioStreamPlayer). If nothing happens when things overlap Check in this order: (1) Is there a CollisionShape2D with an actual Shape assigned? (2) Did you connect the signal, and is it the right one ( vs )? (3) Do the layers and masks let them see each other? (4) Turn on Debug → Visible Collision Shapes and look.

h: Smoothing (the difference between "camera" and "glued to head")
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day How to make the screen follow the player. The moment a team's level (TileMapLayer) is bigger than one screen, they need this. Zero code required for the basic version. The zero-code version 1. Open your Player scene (CharacterBody2D). 2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player. 3. Done. A Camera2D in the scene tree is active automatically, and because it's a child, it goes wherever the player goes. Only one camera wins If two Camera2Ds are active, the most recently entered one takes over. If the view snaps somewhere weird, search the scene tree for a second camera (often left in Main from an earlier experiment). Stop showing the void: limits Without limits, the camera happily shows the empty gray space past the edge of your level. Clamp it, in the Inspector under Limit: Left: , Top: (if your level starts at the origin) Right: level width in pixels, Bottom: level height in pixels How to find the numbers: level width = tiles across × tile size. A 100-tile-wide level of 16px tiles → Right = . Or click the far edge of your level in the editor and read the position in the toolbar. The camera now stops at the edges while the player walks up to them — like Mario. Smoothing (the difference between "camera" and "glued to head") Inspector → Position Smoothing → Enabled ✓. The camera now eases toward the player instead of tracking it rigidly. Speed ≈ = dreamy, ≈ = default-ish, ≈ = tight. This one checkbox is a big Juice and Game Feel win. Smoothing + limits jitter If the camera stutters at level edges, also check Limit → Smoothed ✓. Platformer camera recipe Side-scrollers (Platformer Physics) need more than "glued to the player" — jumping makes a rigid camera bounce nauseatingly. Three Inspector tweaks fix it: 1. Drag margins — stop tracking every jump. Inspector → Drag: Vertical Enabled ✓, then set Top Margin ≈ and Bottom Margin ≈ . Now the camera ignores small vertical moves (normal jumps stay inside the margin box) and only scrolls when the player actually climbs or falls far. This one change is 80% of a good platformer camera. Leave Horizontal Enabled off — you do want tight left/right tracking. Turn on Editor → Draw Drag Margin ✓ to see the box while tuning. 2. Offset the view upward. Players care about what's ahead and above, not the ground under their feet. Inspector → Offset → y = (or so) shifts the view up. 3. Smoothing on, as in the section above — Speed ≈ for platformers. Look-ahead (optional, scripted): shift the camera toward where the player is heading so they can see what's coming. Attach to the Camera2D: — returns -1 or 1, so the offset flips with the run direction. — eases the offset over instead of snapping it. Turn down if direction changes feel swimmy. If you also used the screen-shake script below, put both in one script — they both write to (shake wins while shaking is fine: add the shake to instead of overwriting). Full platformer settings at a glance: child of Player · Limits set · Position Smoothing ✓ (8) · Drag Vertical ✓ (0.7 / 0.2) · Offset y −40. Zoom Inspector → Zoom. = twice as close (pixel-art games usually want this), = zoomed out. Keep x and y equal. For pixel art that looks blurry when zoomed: Project Settings → Rendering → Textures → Default Texture Filter → Nearest. Screen shake (tiny code, big payoff) The one camera feature worth scripting. Attach to the Camera2D: Call it from anywhere via the player, e.g. in a hit handler (Area2D): shakes the view without touching the camera's real position — limits and following keep working. Bigger = harder hit. 4 for a coin, 10 for damage, 20 for an explosion. More ideas in Juice and Game Feel. Fixed camera (single-screen games) Making a one-screen arcade game (like Day 1's)? You don't need a Camera2D at all — the default view is the screen. Only add one when the level outgrows the window.

h: What people actually do with a CharacterBody2D
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day The go-to node for anything the player controls (or any enemy that walks around and hits walls). It's a physics body that you move with code — the engine handles the "don't walk through walls" part. Builds on Movement and Input and Area2D. What CharacterBody2D is (and isn't) Godot has three kinds of 2D physics bodies: — never moves. Walls, floors, Obstacles. No script needed. — moved by your code via . Players, enemies. — moved by the physics engine (gravity, bouncing). Skip it for camp games — it fights you. An is not a body — it detects overlaps but can't be blocked by anything. That's why the Day 1 Area2D player can't have solid walls (see Obstacles). Scene setup, step by step 1. Scene → New Scene, click Other Node, pick CharacterBody2D. Rename it . 2. Add a child: Sprite2D (or AnimatedSprite2D). Drag a texture into its Texture slot. 3. Add a child: CollisionShape2D. In the Inspector, set Shape to a CapsuleShape2D (or Rectangle/Circle) and size it to roughly match the sprite. 4. Save as . The yellow warning triangle A CharacterBody2D with no CollisionShape2D (or a CollisionShape2D with an empty Shape) shows a ⚠️ in the Scene dock and won't collide with anything. Same #1 mistake as Area2D. Setting up input actions Before writing movement code, name your inputs. Project → Project Settings → Input Map: 1. Type in the "Add New Action" box, click Add. 2. Click the + next to the action, press the key (A or ←), click OK. 3. Repeat for , , (and if you need it — see Platformer Physics). Basic movement (top-down) Attach a script to the Player root: That's the whole thing. Notes: is built into CharacterBody2D — don't declare , it already exists. uses automatically (no arguments) and slides along walls instead of stopping dead. is already normalized — diagonals aren't faster. It replaces the four statements from Movement and Input. Movement goes in , not — it runs in sync with the physics engine. For jumping and gravity instead of top-down, see Platformer Physics. What people actually do with a CharacterBody2D The player, top-down or platformer (Platformer Physics). Walking enemies — a patroller that turns at walls, or a chaser that steers at you every frame. Anything that must not pass through walls but isn't controlled by physics — an escort NPC, a pushable-but-scripted crate. Three helpers you get for free after calling : And for reacting to what you hit: Collision layers and masks Every physics body has a Layer ("what am I?") and a Mask ("what do I look at?"), set in Inspector → Collision. A collision happens only if A's mask includes B's layer. The full scheme — the layer names to use, the layer/mask table for every scene type in this reference, the Hurtbox pattern, and the debugging table — lives in one place: Collision Layers and Masks. For a Day 1 or Day 2 game the defaults are fine; go read that note the first time something passes through a wall it shouldn't. The short version for a player: Scene | Layer | Mask | Player (CharacterBody2D) | player | obstacles | Player's Hurtbox (child Area2D) | (none) | mobs, hazards | Give the body a child Area2D named to detect damage. Moving solidly and noticing hits are two different jobs — don't make one node do both.

h: Step 1: name your layers (do this once)
Step 3: how to actually set them
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day The system that decides which things are allowed to touch which things. Every Area2D, CharacterBody2D, and StaticBody2D has these two settings. This note is the single source of truth for them — the other notes link here instead of repeating the table. The mantra Layer = what am I? — the group this object belongs to. Mask = what do I look at? — the groups this object reacts to. A collision or overlap only happens if A's mask includes B's layer. That's it. Everything below is applying that one rule. It is not symmetric A can see B without B seeing A. That's a feature, not a bug — it's how a coin notices the player without the player being shoved by the coin. Step 1: name your layers (do this once) Project → Project Settings → Layer Names → 2D Physics. Naming them turns an unreadable grid of checkboxes into something you can actually reason about. # | Name | What lives here | 1 | player | the player body | 2 | mobs | enemies, mobs, anything that hurts you by touch | 3 | obstacles | walls, floor, TileMapLayer, Obstacles | 4 | bullets | every bullet, player-fired or enemy-fired (Making Bullets) | 5 | hazards | lava, spikes, saw blades (Hazards) | 6 | pickups | coins, hearts, keys (Collectables) | Use this scheme for the whole camp. Every other note in this reference assumes it. Step 2: set each scene Scene | Node type | Layer | Mask | Player | CharacterBody2D | player | obstacles | Player's Hurtbox | Area2D child | (none) | mobs, hazards, bullets | Enemy / Mob | CharacterBody2D | mobs | obstacles | Enemy's Hurtbox | Area2D child | (none) | bullets | Wall / TileMapLayer | StaticBody2D | obstacles | (none) | Coin / Key / Heart | Area2D | pickups | player | Lava / Spikes | Area2D | hazards | player | Player bullet | Area2D | bullets | mobs, obstacles | Enemy bullet | Area2D | bullets | player, obstacles | What this scheme buys you: Player and mobs both stop at walls — both masks include obstacles. The player doesn't physically shove mobs — the player's mask has no mobs. Touching an enemy is handled by a Hurtbox and a signal, so you decide what "getting hit" means. Coins only react to the player, never to an enemy walking over them. A bullet only hits what its mask says. Player bullets mask mobs; enemy bullets mask player. One layer, two behaviours — see Making Bullets. Step 3: how to actually set them Select the node → Inspector → Collision. Two rows of checkboxes: Layer on top, Mask below. Hover any box and Godot shows the name you gave it in Step 1. To set them in code (rarely needed, but useful for a bullet fired by either side): The numbers are the layer numbers from the table, not bitmasks. turns one off. The Hurtbox pattern Moving solidly and detecting "I got hit" are two different jobs. Don't make one node do both — give the body a child Area2D whose only job is detecting: A hurtbox receives damage. A hitbox deals it. Mobs get the mirror image: a body on layer mobs, and a hurtbox masking bullets. Debugging Turn on the X-ray Debug → Visible Collision Shapes, then run the game. Every shape draws as a cyan outline. Ninety percent of "collision isn't working" is solved in ten seconds by seeing that a shape is missing, tiny, or offset from the sprite. Symptom | Cause | Walks through walls | The wall's layer isn't in the walker's mask | Nothing happens on overlap | Missing CollisionShape2D, or an empty Shape slot | Gets stuck on things it shouldn't | A mask box is checked that shouldn't be | Bullet kills the thing that fired it | Shooter's hurtbox masks its own bullet layer | Player shoves mobs around | mobs is in the player's mask — uncheck it |

🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day The node that gives a physics node its body. On its own it does nothing — it's always a child of an Area2D, CharacterBody2D, or StaticBody2D, and it tells that parent what shape it is. The #1 mistake in the whole camp A physics node with no CollisionShape2D, or with an empty Shape slot, detects and collides with nothing. Godot warns you with a ⚠️ triangle in the Scene dock. Click the triangle — it tells you exactly what's wrong. Adding one 1. Select the Area2D / CharacterBody2D / StaticBody2D. 2. + Add Child Node → . 3. In the Inspector, click the Shape dropdown (it says ) and pick a shape. This second step is the one everyone forgets. 4. In the 2D viewport, drag the orange dots to resize it over your sprite. Which shape to pick Shape | Use for | Notes | RectangleShape2D | crates, platforms, walls, most UI-ish triggers | Fastest. Default choice for anything boxy. | CircleShape2D | coins, balls, bombs, pickups | Best for a Bouncing Ball — bounces are predictable. | CapsuleShape2D | players and humanoid enemies | Rounded ends stop the player catching on tile seams. Use this for platformer players. | SegmentShape2D | laser lines, thin beams | Rare. | ConvexPolygonShape2D | odd rigid shapes | Must be convex (no dents). | ConcavePolygonShape2D | complex static geometry | Static only — never put it on something that moves. | There's also , a separate node where you click points to draw a custom outline. Handy for a weird-shaped platform; overkill for most camp games. Sizing it well The shape matters more than the sprite for how the game feels. Slightly smaller than the sprite for the player's hurtbox — near misses feel fair and generous. Slightly larger than the sprite for pickups — grabbing a coin feels satisfying instead of finicky. Match the sprite for walls and platforms, or the world looks like it's lying to you. See what you're doing Debug → Visible Collision Shapes, then press Play. Every shape draws in cyan while the game runs. This is how you catch a shape that's the right size but offset three pixels off the sprite. Turning one off (safely) You'll want this for i-frames, a dash that passes through enemies, or a door that unlocks. Never set directly during a collision callback — the physics engine is mid-step and Godot will spam an error. Use : For a Area2D you can also just turn off the whole area: One node, many shapes A parent can have several CollisionShape2D children and they simply add together. Useful for an L-shaped platform, or a boss made of two overlapping circles — easier than fighting with a polygon. The trick Select a CollisionShape2D on a StaticBody2D platform → Inspector → check One Way Collision. The player can now jump up through the platform but lands on top of it. Two clicks, and your platformer instantly feels like a real one. See Platformer Physics.

b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 4 - Production Day, Day 5 - Polish and Showcase The nodes that put text and buttons on the screen. CanvasLayer pins things to the screen so they don't scroll with the world. Label shows text. For the score system built on top of these, see Score and UI. Always start with a CanvasLayer A Label placed directly in the world will slide off screen the moment your Camera2D moves. A CanvasLayer draws on a separate layer that ignores the camera entirely. Rule: if the player should always see it, it goes under a CanvasLayer. Score, lives, timers, menus, pause screens. Label Add a Label, type into Text in the Inspector, drag it into place. is not optional errors — you can't add a number to text. works. This is the single most common GDScript error of the week. Two nicer ways to build the string: Making a Label readable Default Labels are small, white, and vanish against a bright background. In the Inspector: Theme Overrides → Font Sizes → Font Size — bump it to 32+. Theme Overrides → Colors → Font Color — pick something that contrasts. Theme Overrides → Constants → Outline Size = , then Colors → Font Outline Color = black. An outline makes text legible over any background. Do this once on every Label; it's the cheapest polish in the game. Horizontal/Vertical Alignment — set to Center, then size the Label box, rather than nudging position by hand. Anchors: keeping UI in the corner Select the Label → the Anchor Preset button in the toolbar (looks like a box with red pins). Pick Top Left for a score, Center for a "GAME OVER" message, Bottom Right for a timer. Anchored UI stays put no matter what resolution the game runs at — which matters on Friday when your game is on a projector instead of your laptop. Button Connect the signal. Style it the same way as a Label via Theme Overrides. Full menu flow in Scene Switching. Marker2D: an X on the map
What people actually do with a Marker2D

Node2D is an empty thing with a position — every other 2D node is built on it. Marker2D is a Node2D you can actually see in the editor, used to mark a spot. Node2D: what every 2D node inherits Every property below works on CharacterBody2D, Area2D, , all of them — because they're all Node2Ds underneath. vs is measured from the parent. If your Bullet is a child of the Gun, setting puts it on the gun, not at the world origin. When something looks like it teleported to the top-left corner, this is almost always why. Use when you mean "this exact spot in the world." What people actually do with a plain Node2D 1. As a container to organize the scene tree. Free, costs nothing, makes a messy scene readable: 2. As a group handle — move the parent, move everything. This is the trick behind Enemy Formations: put fifty aliens under one Node2D, move the Node2D, and all fifty march in perfect formation with one script instead of fifty. 3. To clear a whole category at once: 4. As a pivot to rotate around. Rotating a child rotates it in place; rotating its parent swings the child around the parent. That's how you make an orbiting shield or a swinging spike ball: Marker2D: an X on the map A Node2D that draws a little cross in the editor so you can see and drag it. It has no effect on the running game — it's purely a named position. What people actually do with a Marker2D Spawn points. Add as a child of the gun, drag it to the barrel tip: Now a designer moves the barrel tip by dragging in the editor — no code change. See Making Bullets. Patrol endpoints. Drop and , drag them where you want the enemy to walk. Full build in Patrol Enemies. Player start / respawn point. Drop a marker in each level: Used by Health and Lives and Hazards. Camera anchors, door destinations, checkpoints — anywhere you'd otherwise hardcode and regret it. Make markers children of the level, not the moving thing A patrol marker parented to the enemy travels with the enemy, so the enemy chases a target it can never reach. Parent patrol and spawn markers to the level root. (Muzzle markers are the exception — those should ride along with the gun.) h: The whole family, in one table
What people actually do with it
What people actually do with it
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day The other two physics bodies. CharacterBody2D gets the spotlight because you control it, but these two do real work: StaticBody2D is every wall in your game, and RigidBody2D is what the Day 1 mobs actually are. The whole family, in one table Node | Who moves it | Use it for | StaticBody2D | nobody — it never moves | walls, floors, platforms, crates, Obstacles | CharacterBody2D | your code, via | player, walking enemies | RigidBody2D | the physics engine — gravity, forces, bounces | falling crates, drifting mobs, real bouncing balls | AnimatableBody2D | your code, but it pushes things | Moving Platforms, elevators | Area2D | not a body at all | detection only — see Area2D | StaticBody2D The simplest node in Godot. Add it, give it a CollisionShape2D, done — no script, ever. Layer obstacles, mask (none) — see Collision Layers and Masks. A wall doesn't need to look for anything; the things that move look for it. What people actually do with it Level geometry. Though if you have more than a handful of walls, paint a TileMapLayer instead — it generates all this for you. One-way platforms. Select the CollisionShape2D → check One Way Collision. Jump up through, land on top. Two clicks. Slippery ice / conveyor belts. Inspector → Physics Material Override → New PhysicsMaterial2D → set Friction to . A bouncy wall. Same Physics Material, Bounce to . Only affects RigidBody2D; a CharacterBody2D needs the code in Bouncing Ball. Solid hazards. A spike block is a StaticBody2D (blocks you) plus a child Area2D (hurts you). See Hazards. Moving a StaticBody2D You can change its in code, but it won't push anything — the player will be shoved out or squished unpredictably. If it moves and carries the player, you want AnimatableBody2D (Moving Platforms). RigidBody2D You don't move a RigidBody2D. You nudge it and let the engine take over — gravity, momentum, bouncing, spinning, all for free. That freedom is exactly why it's a bad fit for a player character: you ask it to stop, and it argues. The Day 1 mob Dodge the Creeps mobs are RigidBody2Ds. They get one velocity at spawn and drift forever: That is the setting students always miss when they add a new mob type — the mob falls straight off the bottom of the screen. See Homing Enemies for the version that chases you instead. Key Inspector properties Property | What it does | Gravity Scale | = normal fall, = floats, = falls up | Mass | heavier things get shoved less | Physics Material → Bounce | = thud, = bounces forever | Physics Material → Friction | = ice | Linear Damp | air resistance; slows it over time | Lock Rotation | stops it tumbling — usually what you want | Freeze | pause it entirely until you unfreeze | Pushing it around What people actually do with it Physics crates the player can shove around. A bomb or grenade you toss with and let arc naturally. Falling debris for juice (Juice and Game Feel). A real bouncing ball — Bounce , Gravity Scale , Linear Damp , one impulse at start. This is the lazy way to build Pong; Bouncing Ball shows the controllable way and explains why you'd want it. Don't set on a RigidBody2D Teleporting one fights the physics engine and causes jitter or tunneling. If you must move it directly, you probably wanted a CharacterBody2D. Detecting a hit RigidBody2D doesn't report collisions by default. Inspector → check Contact Monitor, set Max Contacts Reported to or more, then connect (Signals). Forgetting this pair of settings is the classic "my RigidBody signal never fires" bug.

🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day How to paint a whole level — floors, walls, platforms — instead of dragging in fifty StaticBody2D walls one at a time. Tiles can carry their own collision, so the level is solid for free. Pairs with CharacterBody2D and Camera2D. The pieces — the node you paint on. One layer of tiles (add more TileMapLayer nodes for background/foreground). — a resource that holds your tile images and their collision shapes. Lives inside the TileMapLayer's Inspector. Atlas — one image containing many tiles in a grid (e.g. a 16×16-per-tile sheet). This is how most free tile art comes (Asset Resources). TileMap vs TileMapLayer Older tutorials use a node called TileMap — it's deprecated. In our Godot (4.6) use TileMapLayer. Everything works the same; one node per layer instead of one node with internal layers. Setup, step by step 1. Add the node. In your Main scene, add a child → TileMapLayer. Rename it . 2. Create the TileSet. With selected: Inspector → Tile Set → → New TileSet. Click it to expand and set Tile Size to match your art (e.g. 16×16 — check the asset pack's description). 3. Add your tile art. Two panels open at the bottom of the editor: TileSet panel (bottom) — where you define tiles. TileMap panel (bottom) — where you paint tiles. Open the TileSet panel and drag your tilesheet PNG from the FileSystem dock into the left column. When Godot asks "Would you like to automatically create tiles in the atlas?" → Yes. It slices the image into tiles on its own. 4. Paint. Switch to the TileMap panel, click a tile to select it, then click/drag in the viewport to paint. Hold Right-click to erase. Rect tool (in the panel toolbar) fills big areas fast. Painting quality of life - Hold Shift while clicking to draw a straight line of tiles. - Pick the eyedropper in the TileMap panel to grab a tile already painted in the level. - If the grid doesn't match your art (tiles look cut off), the Tile Size from step 2 is wrong. Making tiles solid (collision) Painted tiles are just pictures until you give them physics: 1. Select the node → Inspector → expand Tile Set. 2. Physics Layers → Add Element. This creates physics layer 0 on the TileSet. Set its Collision Layer to your world layer (see CharacterBody2D) and clear its Mask. 3. Open the TileSet panel (bottom) → click Select mode → click a tile that should be solid. 4. In the tile's properties, expand Physics → Physics Layer 0. A drawing area appears — the default is a full square covering the tile. That's usually exactly what you want; click the tile and the square shape is added. 5. Repeat for every solid tile (walls, ground). Leave decorations (grass, flowers, background) with no physics. Now a CharacterBody2D with world in its mask stops on those tiles automatically. No walls to build, no script on the level at all. "My player falls through the floor" Check, in order: (1) Did you add a physics layer to the TileSet (step 2)? (2) Does the tile you painted with have a collision polygon (steps 3–5)? (3) Does the player's mask include the TileSet's collision layer? Painting with the one tile you forgot to give physics is the classic version of this bug. Placing tiles from code (optional) You rarely need this, but for procedural stuff: — which atlas (0 if you only added one image). — which tile within the sheet, in tile units: is top-left. Multiple layers Add more TileMapLayer nodes for depth — order in the scene tree = draw order (lower in the tree draws on top):

Pattern 3: a cooldown (can I shoot yet?)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Node Info Index · Used on Day 1 - Meet Godot, Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 4 - Production Day A node that counts down and then fires a signal. It's how anything in your game happens later or repeatedly — spawning, cooldowns, invincibility, "you win after 30 seconds." The three Inspector settings that matter Property | What it does | Wait Time | seconds to count down | Autostart | starts by itself when the scene loads | One Shot | on = fires once and stops. off = repeats forever | Then connect the signal to a function (Signals). Pattern 1: repeat forever Wait Time , Autostart on, One Shot off. This is the backbone of Spawning and Timers. Pattern 2: do something once, later Autostart off, One Shot on. Start it from code: also accepts an override: counts 2.5 seconds regardless of Wait Time. Pattern 3: a cooldown (can I shoot yet?) The most useful Timer pattern in the whole reference. One Shot on, Autostart off. returns when the timer isn't running — so "is the cooldown over?" Change Wait Time to change fire rate. Same shape as the dash cooldown in Dash and Double Jump and the i-frames in Health and Lives. Useful methods A countdown display, using Label and CanvasLayer: The one-line version: For a quick pause you don't want a whole node for: pauses just this function for 0.2 seconds while the rest of the game keeps running. Perfect for hit flashes and short delays. Use a real Timer node when you need to check, restart, or cancel it — use for fire-and-forget. A gotcha with If the node gets d during the wait, the code after runs on a dead node and errors. Guard it: . h: The simpler alternative (use it when you can)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index How to keep score, lives, and settings alive across scene changes. The partner note to Scene Switching. A script that is always loaded, in every scene, and never destroyed. It's the answer to "how do I keep the score when I go to the next level?" — a question Scene Switching raises three times and defers to an instructor. This is that answer. The problem it solves destroys the old scene and everything in it. Your score variable lived in the old scene. It's gone. An autoload lives outside all scenes, so it survives the switch. Setting one up 1. Create a new script anywhere in the project. Call it . Don't attach it to anything. 2. Project → Project Settings → Globals → Autoload tab. 3. Click the folder icon, pick . 4. Node Name: . Click Add. That's it. Now works from any script in the project, with no path and no . Name it something obvious , , or . The Node Name field is what you type in code — if you name it you will regret it by Thursday. A game state autoload Use it from anywhere — no path, no reference, no setup: Wiring the UI to it Each scene connects to the autoload's signals when it loads: That second line matters — connecting only tells you about future changes, so call it once manually to display what's already there. Always reset before a new game never resets by itself. Without on your title screen's Start button, the second playthrough begins with the first one's score and zero lives. This is the #1 autoload bug. What belongs in an autoload Good: Score, lives, current level, unlocked abilities Settings — music volume, difficulty Saved data (High Scores That Persist) A music player that keeps playing across scene changes (below) Bad: The player node, or anything visual — those belong in the scene Everything, because it's convenient. An autoload that knows about all of your game becomes the tangle every bug lives in Music that survives scene changes The classic use, and it's three lines. Make an autoload scene instead of a bare script: a root with an AudioStreamPlayer child, saved as , then autoload the scene file. Without this, changing scenes restarts your music from the top every time — which sounds broken. The simpler alternative (use it when you can) You often don't need an autoload at all. If your levels are just swapped tilemaps inside one persistent Main scene — the pattern in Scene Switching — the player and score are never destroyed, so nothing needs saving. Rule: if you can avoid changing scenes, avoid the autoload too. Reach for this when you genuinely have separate Title / Game / Game Over scenes and need something to survive between them. h: Why not just use a RigidBody2D?
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day A ball that flies around and bounces off walls — Pong, Breakout, Arkanoid, and any game with a projectile that ricochets. Built on CharacterBody2D and . Why not just use a RigidBody2D? You can. Set Bounce to , Gravity Scale to , Linear Damp to , kick it once, and the engine does it (RigidBody2D and StaticBody2D). But you'll fight it. Pong needs the ball to keep a constant speed forever, to speed up over time, and to change angle based on where it hit the paddle. A RigidBody2D bleeds energy, gets stuck in horizontal loops, and won't let you set those rules. Twelve lines of your own code gives you total control. Rule of thumb: physics ball for a toy, coded ball for a game. The ball scene Scene → New Scene → Other Node → CharacterBody2D, name it , save as . Use a circle. A rectangle ball catches on corners and produces bounces that look wrong. The core script That's the whole mechanic. The important bits: , not . Slide is for characters — it slides along walls, which is the exact opposite of bouncing. stops at the impact and hands you the collision. does the reflection math for you. The normal is the arrow pointing straight out of the surface you hit; mirrors your velocity around it. This is the one line people expect to be hard. Re-normalizing to every bounce is what keeps a constant, arcade-feeling pace. Without it the ball slowly drifts faster or slower. Walls are plain StaticBody2Ds on layer obstacles (RigidBody2D and StaticBody2D), or a TileMapLayer with collision. Pong: paddles and English The magic of Pong isn't the bounce — it's that where the ball hits the paddle changes the angle. That's what turns it from a physics demo into a game with skill. The paddle is a CharacterBody2D on layer obstacles: on the action names means one paddle scene serves both players — drag in two instances and set / on one and / on the other in the Inspector. Add all four to Project Settings → Input Map. Now replace the ball's bounce block to handle paddles specially: Put both paddles in a group called (Node dock → Groups). Hit the paddle's center and the ball goes back flat; hit the edge and it fires off at a steep angle. That one rule is the entire game of Pong. Scoring: goal zones An Area2D behind each paddle, stretched to cover the whole side: And in the ball: Display the score with Label and CanvasLayer. Breakout: bricks that break Same ball, different targets. A brick is a StaticBody2D on layer obstacles with a script: In the ball's collision handler: is a nice trick — the ball doesn't need to know what a brick is, only that it knows how to be destroyed. Walls don't have , so they just bounce. Lay out a grid of bricks from code so you're not dragging fifty by hand: is a plain Node2D container. Win when . Common problems Problem | Fix | Ball sticks to a wall and vibrates | You used . Use . | Ball tunnels straight through a wall at high speed | Cap , thicken the walls, or turn on the ball's Continuous CD in the Inspector | Ball gets stuck bouncing perfectly horizontally, forever | After bouncing, force a minimum vertical component (below) | Ball speeds up until it's invisible | You forgot | Bounces look wrong / catch on corners | Use a CircleShape2D, not a rectangle | The anti-horizontal fix, worth adding to any Pong: Where else this shows up Bouncing bullets — a shot that ricochets off walls (Making Bullets). A bouncing enemy — a slime that ping-pongs around the room. Breakout powerups — a brick drops a collectable that widens the paddle.

h: Making it feel good (do this, it takes 3 minutes)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day Coins, gems, stars, hearts, keys — anything the player runs into and picks up. This is the single best first mechanic to add to a game. It takes about ten minutes, it works in every genre, and it instantly gives a game a reason to explore. Built on Area2D and Signals. The coin scene Scene → New Scene → Other Node → Area2D. Name it , save as . Layers are from Collision Layers and Masks — the coin lives on pickups and watches player, so mobs can walk right over it. Make the shape bigger than the sprite A pickup radius slightly larger than the coin art makes collecting feel generous instead of fiddly. This is a real design decision, not laziness. The coin script Connect the Area2D's signal to this function (Signals). shows up in the Inspector — drop a coin worth and a gem worth from the same scene by changing one number per instance. No second scene needed. — put the player in a group via Node dock → Groups → → Add. More robust than checking the name (Area2D explains why). deletes the coin so it disappears. Counting them: the group approach The easiest way to keep score without wiring up signals for every coin. In your Main script: Add every coin to a group called : select the Coin in the coin scene → Node dock → Groups → . Every instance inherits it, so you can drag fifty coins into the level and they all wire themselves up. See Score and UI and Label and CanvasLayer. Why and not doesn't remove the node until the end of the frame, so the coin that just fired the signal is still in the list when you count. Off-by-one "I collected them all but nothing happened" bugs live here. Making it feel good (do this, it takes 3 minutes) A silent coin that blinks out is forgettable. Replace with: The coin swells, floats up, fades out, and dings. Same three lines of tween work anywhere — see Tweens and Juice and Game Feel. A gentle idle bob (no code) Select the Coin → add an AnimationPlayer → new animation , 1 second, Loop on and Autoplay on. Key at 0s and 1s, and at 0.5s. Now every coin in your game breathes. Coins that move catch the eye far better than coins that sit still. Or in three lines of code: Variations A magnet — coins fly toward a nearby player: A heart that heals — same scene, different script, wired to Health and Lives: A key — see Doors and Keys. A powerup with a timer — grant an ability, then take it back: Note this one can't immediately — it has to stay alive to undo itself. Hide the sprite and disable the shape instead, then free it after. Coins that spawn over time — combine with Spawning and Timers. A collectable that unlocks the exit — the win condition of half the games at showcase.

h: Coyote time (the one every platformer needs)
A cooldown the player can see
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 4 - Production Day, Day 5 - Polish and Showcase Two abilities that make a platformer feel good to control. Both are short, both bolt onto the script in Platformer Physics, and both are the kind of thing playtesters notice immediately. Uses Timer and CharacterBody2D. Add these after your game works These are feel upgrades, not features. Get the level, the enemies, and the win condition working first — then spend twenty minutes here and watch the game get twice as fun. Double Jump The idea You already have gating your jump. A double jump just means counting jumps instead of asking about the floor. (not ) is essential — otherwise holding the button burns every jump in one frame. Make the second jump readable The air jump should look different from the ground jump, or players won't realize they have one: More in Tweens and Juice and Game Feel. Coyote time (the one every platformer needs) Players constantly press jump a frame or two after walking off a ledge, and a game that refuses feels stiff and unfair. Give them a grace window. Add a (Timer, One Shot on, Wait Time ): Nobody will ever say "I love your coyote time." They'll say the controls feel good. That's the point. Variable jump height Tap for a short hop, hold for a full jump. Two lines: Coyote time and variable jump height together are the two highest-value additions to any platformer in this camp. Dash The idea A dash is a short burst at high speed in a fixed direction, with a cooldown. Three pieces of state: are we dashing, which way, and can we dash again yet. Add two Timer nodes, both One Shot on, Autostart off: — Wait Time (how long the dash lasts) — Wait Time (how long until you can dash again) Add to Project Settings → Input Map (Shift is the convention). The cooldown check is the same Timer pattern as a weapon's fire rate in Making Bullets — once students have it, they reuse it everywhere. Invincible dash Let the player dash through enemies. Wire it to the hurtbox from Health and Lives: This changes the dash from a movement tool into a defensive skill, and instantly makes combat more interesting. Great design conversation: the same mechanic can be about getting somewhere or about surviving, depending on one flag. Air dash (one per jump) Air dash plus double jump gives a platformer a real movement vocabulary — suddenly there are multiple ways to cross a gap, and level design gets more interesting. The ghost trail The cheapest way to make a dash look expensive: Call it every couple of frames while dashing: Also worth adding: a short Camera2D shake and a brief slow-motion via (Juice and Game Feel). A cooldown the player can see A ProgressBar under a CanvasLayer (Label and CanvasLayer). Players will use an ability far more often when they can see it's ready. Common problems Problem | Fix | Dash never stops | 's isn't connected, or One Shot is off | Dashes forever while holding the key | Use , not | Dash goes nowhere when standing still | Add the fallback direction based on facing | Player rockets off after dashing | Add on dash end | Double jump gives infinite jumps | is being reset somewhere every frame — check it's only reset when | Dash phases through walls | handles it; if it still tunnels, lower or thicken walls |

🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day A door that won't open until you find the key. This is the smallest possible progression mechanic — and progression is what turns a room full of stuff into a level. Builds on Collectables and Area2D. Why this mechanic matters Coins give the player something to do. A locked door gives them a reason to explore. The instant you add one, your level has structure: this part first, then that part. Teams that add a key and a door on Day 4 almost always end up with a better-feeling game than teams that add more enemies. The key A collectable that sets a flag instead of adding score. means one key scene handles gold, blue, and red keys — set it per instance in the Inspector. The player holds the keys In the player script: A Dictionary ( ) maps color → how many you're carrying. reads a count and returns if you've never picked that color up, instead of erroring. returns / , so the door can ask "may I open?" and get an answer in one line. Declare at the top to drive a UI display (Label and CanvasLayer). Simplest possible version If dictionaries feel like too much for your team, use on the player and be done. You lose multiple key colors and gain ten minutes. That's often the right trade on Day 4. The door A door needs to do two things: block the player, and notice them. That's two nodes (Area2D can't block, StaticBody2D can't detect): The three things that make this feel good: on the shape — disabling a CollisionShape2D during a collision callback errors without it. — the door shakes when it's locked. Without feedback, players think the game is broken. Three lines, huge difference. The locked sound. A locked door that's silent reads as a bug. Add to Project Settings → Input Map (E is the convention) if you use manual opening. Showing what you're carrying If the player can't see they have the key, they won't think to go back to the door. Variations worth stealing A door to the next level — no key, just an exit (Scene Switching): Collect-them-all gate — the exit opens once every coin is gone.
