h: The player side: taking the hit
Option A: paint visuals, stretch an Area2D (simplest)
Option B: solid hazard tiles (spikes you stand on)
Option C: walk-in hazard tiles with Custom Data (real lava)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day Things that hurt the player on touch — lava, spikes, poison pools, saw blades. The counterpart to Obstacles (which block but don't hurt). Builds on Area2D and CharacterBody2D. The idea A hazard is just an Area2D that calls on the player. It doesn't block movement — the player can walk into lava (that's the point). If you also want it solid (a spiky wall), you combine it with a StaticBody2D — see the spike block at the bottom. Hazards live on the hazards layer and mask player. The full layer scheme for the whole camp is in Collision Layers and Masks — set it up once there and every note in this reference lines up. Basic lava pit New scene: Area2D root named : Connect the Area2D's signal (Signals) and attach: That's the whole script. Because the mask is player only, can never be a mob or a bullet — no checks needed, same trick as Making Bullets. Make the shape slightly smaller than the art Pull the CollisionShape2D in a few pixels from the lava's visual edge. Players feel like they died fairly when the hitbox is forgiving; pixel-perfect lava feels cheap. This is a real game-design trick, not a hack. The player side: taking the hit The hazard's whole job is to report the damage. The player decides what that means — lose a heart, respawn, game over. That logic belongs in one place, on the player, so every hazard, mob, and bullet in your game shares it. That code lives in Health and Lives: , invincibility frames, hearts, respawning, and checkpoints. Build it once there and every hazard on this page works. The two things worth repeating here, because hazards are where they bite hardest: 1. Invincibility frames are not optional for hazards. Standing in lava fires the damage call every physics frame — sixty hits a second, three hearts gone instantly. The guard in Health and Lives is what makes a hazard feel fair instead of broken. 2. Reset velocity on respawn. Without , a player who fell into a pit respawns still travelling at full falling speed and immediately dies again. If your team hasn't built the health system yet, the two-line version is enough to get a hazard working today: Lava in a tile-based level Three ways to make tiles dangerous, from simplest to most flexible. Pick one. Option A: paint visuals, stretch an Area2D (simplest) Paint the lava tiles as pure visuals (no physics on those tiles), then stretch one Lava Area2D from above over the whole pool. One hazard, one shape, easy to see and debug. Best when you have a few big pools. Option B: solid hazard tiles (spikes you stand on) Hazard tiles that are solid — the player lands on them and gets hurt. Good for spike strips and thorn floors. 1. Add a second TileMapLayer node named next to your layer (see TileMapLayer). Keeping hazards on their own node is the trick — it lets the player tell lava apart from ordinary ground. 2. Give it its own TileSet (or reuse the same one) with a physics layer whose Collision Layer = hazards (TileMapLayer). 3. Select the node → Node dock → Groups → add it to a group called . 4. Make sure the player's mask includes hazards so actually collides with these tiles. 5. Paint your spikes on , normal ground on . Player side — after , ask what we bumped into: / — everything touched this frame. returns the node we hit — the layer — and the group check identifies it. Walls on aren't in the group, so they stay harmless. Option C: walk-in hazard tiles with Custom Data (real lava) Lava you can walk into — not solid, hurts while you're in it. This is the "proper" Godot way and it scales to any number of pools with zero extra nodes. Mark the tiles: 1. Select your TileMapLayer → Inspector → expand Tile Set → Custom Data Layers → Add Element. Name it , Type bool. 2. Open the TileSet panel (bottom) → Select mode → click a lava tile → expand Custom Data → check . 3. Repeat for every dangerous tile. Give lava tiles no physics layer — they shouldn't block. Check the tile the player is standing in: then — converts the player's world position into "which grid cell am I in" (TileMapLayer). returns on empty cells — that's what the guards against. Skip the guard and you crash the first time the player is over an empty cell. is the player's center. For a tall character, check the feet instead: (half the collision shape's height). This runs every frame you're in lava — the invincibility frames in Health and Lives are not optional here. Variants Spikes (hurt + solid): combine both nodes — a StaticBody2D block (Obstacles) with a hazard Area2D child covering just the pointy top: Same one-line script on the Hurtzone. The player can stand beside it safely and gets hurt only from the spiky side. Moving saw blade: put the lava script on an Area2D and animate its position — simplest way is an keyframing back and forth, or the patrol pattern from Movement and Input adapted to an Area2D ( ). Damage-over-time pool (lose a life every second you stand in it) — use / plus a Timer instead of one-shot damage; only reach for this if the design really needs it. "The lava doesn't hurt me" Check, in order: (1) Does the Area2D have a CollisionShape2D with an actual shape? (2) Is the signal connected? (3) Hazard mask includes player's layer? (4) Does the player script actually have a function (Health and Lives)? — the error means it doesn't.

🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day Hearts, HP, getting hurt, invincibility frames, dying, and respawning. This is the note every damage-dealing thing points at — Hazards, Patrol Enemies, and Making Bullets all end in "call ", and this is where that function lives. Where health should live Put it on the player, in the player's own script. Not in a global, not in Main. Everything that hurts the player then calls one function, and there's only one place to debug. Layers come from Collision Layers and Masks. The Hurtbox is a separate Area2D so that moving and getting hit stay separate jobs. The player health script Add this to your existing player script — it sits alongside your movement code, it doesn't replace it. Connect 's signal to (Signals). Why the guard is the first line: without it, standing in lava calls sixty times a second and you lose three hearts instantly. The guard is what makes damage feel fair. The hurtbox connection Connect the Hurtbox's signal: checks whether that node has a property. So a spike can and a boss laser can set , and the player handles both without knowing what hit it. For enemies that are bodies rather than areas, connect the same way. The invincibility flash I-frames the player can't see feel like a bug. Blink during them: Six blinks at 0.16s each ≈ 1 second, matching the Timer. More options in Juice and Game Feel; the tween syntax itself is explained in Tweens. Showing hearts Under a CanvasLayer, an HBoxContainer with one TextureRect per heart (Label and CanvasLayer): In your Main script, listen for the signal instead of checking every frame: Signals, not polling. The UI updates exactly when health changes, and the player script never needs to know the UI exists. That separation is worth pointing out — it's why the same player scene drops into any level. Or a health bar Add a ProgressBar instead: Nicer, animated: Respawning Drop a Marker2D in the level and drag it where the player should appear. That last line matters more than it looks. Respawning without i-frames into a room full of enemies is an instant death loop. Checkpoints An Area2D the player walks through that moves the spawn point: Lives on top of health Health is per-attempt; lives are how many attempts you get. Keep them in Main, not the player: Since the player already respawns itself, Main only decides whether that's allowed to happen again. Enemies with health too Same idea, smaller: A bullet then works on anything: . Player, enemy, breakable crate — all the same call (Making Bullets). Falling out of the world A wide, thin Area2D under the whole level: Common problems Problem | Fix | Lose all hearts in one touch | Missing the guard | Never take damage | Hurtbox mask doesn't include the attacker's layer (Collision Layers and Masks) | Hearts don't update | never connected, or connected after already emitted | Player respawns and dies instantly | Respawn without i-frames, or the spawn point is inside a hazard | Stays half-transparent after i-frames | Reset in the timeout handler | Errors after dying | Code kept running on a freed node — use , not |

The Day 1 tutorial mobs are s that get a velocity once and drift in a straight line forever. A homing mob steers toward the player every frame instead. Builds on Spawning and Timers; the predictable cousin that walks a fixed route is Patrol Enemies, and Enemy States combines the two. Step 1: put the player in a group The mob needs a way to find the player. Groups are the easiest way: 1. Select your Player node. 2. In the Node panel (right side, next to the Inspector) → Groups tab. 3. Type → Add. Now any script in the game can ask for it by name. Do this before anything else — it's the step everyone forgets. Step 2: the homing script Attach this to the mob's root (or duplicate first and attach it to the copy): Line by line: — grabs the player without hardcoding a path like , which breaks the moment a mob is spawned into a different parent. — turns "the player is 300 pixels that way" into a pure direction of length 1, so is the only thing controlling how fast the mob moves. — this is the line that makes it feel good. Snapping straight to the target direction gives you an unavoidable heat-seeker. Lerping gives the mob turning momentum, so a quick sidestep can make it overshoot and swing around. Tune between about and to taste. — stops mobs from swarming your corpse after a hit, since the tutorial hides the player on death. — points the sprite where it's heading. Delete this line if your art shouldn't rotate. Mixing chasers and drifters You don't need two separate mob scenes. Add an exported flag to your existing mob and only run the steering when it's on: Then in your spawn code (Spawning and Timers), flip a coin so some creeps drift and some chase: A field of drifters with the occasional hunter reads as much more dangerous than a field of pure hunters — the player can't tell which is which until it turns. Either let mobs ignore obstacles (mask excludes the obstacles layer, so they pass through) or accept that walls double as mob shields, which honestly can be a fun mechanic. Decide on purpose. None of it changes the rules; all of it changes how the game feels to play. Juice comes last Only add juice once your game runs without crashing and the full start → play → lose → restart loop works. Juice added in a hurry is the #1 way to break a working game right before a showcase. Each effect below is self-contained: it plugs into a script you already have (your hit/game-over function, your pickup script, etc.). Node names are examples — swap in your project's actual names. Camera shake when the player is hit Where it goes: the script on whatever node owns your camera — usually the Player. 1. Select your Player in the Scene dock → → add Camera2D (if you don't already have one). In the Inspector, make sure Enabled is checked. 2. Add this function to that node's script: 3. Call from wherever the hit happens — e.g. inside your or function. 4. Press F5 and get hit — the screen should jitter for a fraction of a second, then settle. — animates a property over time from code, no animation editor needed. The last line resets the camera to center so the game doesn't stay crooked. A quick scale pop when a pickup is collected Where it goes: your pickup's script (the from Area2D). Trigger it in main.gd, wherever your game-over logic runs: 5. Press F5 and die on purpose — you should see a burst of particles right where the player was.

b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day How to shoot things — one reusable bullet scene, then two complete builds: a Space Invaders shooter (you shoot up) and a bullet-dodging boss (it shoots at you). Builds on Area2D and CharacterBody2D. Layer setup first Set up the camp-wide layer names once, from Collision Layers and Masks. Bullets use layer 4 — bullets. The whole trick of this note: a bullet's mask decides what it can hit. Both kinds of bullet sit on the same bullets layer; only the mask differs. Bullet | Layer | Mask | Player's bullet | bullets | mobs, obstacles | Enemy's bullet | bullets | player, obstacles | Nothing else needs an check — if the signal fires, it hit something it was allowed to hit. Give every bullet a VisibleOnScreenNotifier2D Bullets that fly off screen keep existing forever, and the game slowly grinds to a halt. One node, one signal, one line of cleanup — do it now, not when it breaks. The bullet scene (used by both examples) New scene: Area2D root named , with three children: Script on the root — connect both signals in this scene: the Bullet's own , and the Notifier's (Signals): Because the mask only includes mobs, never fires for the player or walls — no group checks needed. That's conditional collision doing the work for you. The Notifier prevents the classic "1,000 invisible bullets flying to infinity" slowdown. Save as . Example 1: Space Invaders (shoot straight up) Aliens come down from the top; the player slides along the bottom and shoots up. Input Map: add a action (Space) next to / . Player script (on a CharacterBody2D — horizontal only): Drag into the slot in the Inspector — forgetting this is the #1 crash ( on null). — remember y is negative-up in 2D (Platformer Physics). The offset spawns the bullet at the ship's nose instead of its center, so it can't clip the shooter. Bullets are added to the current scene, not the player — they keep flying even if the player dies. The aliens: any descending mob on the mobs layer works — reuse the pattern from Spawning and Timers with . Bullet mask = mobs → bullets pop aliens, aliens ignore each other. Fire-rate limit (optional) — hold to shoot, but not a laser hose. Add a child named (Wait Time , One Shot ✓): Example 2: Boss that shoots at the player A boss stands in one place, fires bullets aimed at wherever the player is, and the player dodges. Enemy bullet variant. Duplicate the bullet scene (FileSystem → right-click → Duplicate → ) and change two things in the Inspector: Mask: player (instead of mobs) — now it only hits the player. Different sprite color so players can read danger at a glance. The script is identical — only layers and art change. Adjust its hit code to tell the player it's been hit instead of instantly deleting it: Boss scene: it never moves, so it's simple — no CharacterBody2D needed: Script on the Boss root — connect the Timer's signal (Spawning and Timers): — the aiming line. Target minus me = direction to target; makes it length 1 so stays in charge. Add the player to the "player" group: select the Player root → Node dock → Groups → type → Add. That's how the boss finds it without a hard-coded path. The check stops the boss from crashing (and rudely shooting) after the player dies. Player side: the player needs the function the bullet calls. Build the real one — hearts, i-frames, respawn — in Health and Lives. The bare minimum to get bullets working today: Tuning the dodge: the whole game feel lives in two numbers — boss bullet (slower = more readable, try 300) and wait time (shorter = more frantic). Slow bullets + fast timer = bullet-hell curtain; fast bullets + slow timer = sniper duel. Both are fun; they're different games. Want the player to shoot back? Give the player Example 1's shoot code (aimed with the mouse if you like: ), give the Boss a health variable, and have the player-bullet's call a on it instead of . Boss fight complete. "My bullets hit the wrong things" It's always layers. Player bullet: Layer bullets, Mask mobs. Boss bullet: Layer bullets, Mask player. Neither bullet should mask bullets — otherwise bullets annihilate each other mid-air (which, granted, is a mechanic in some games — do it on purpose or not at all).

b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day Platforms that slide back and forth, elevators, falling platforms, conveyor belts. The classic way to make a platformer level feel alive instead of static. Builds on Platformer Physics and Node2D and Marker2D. Use AnimatableBody2D, not StaticBody2D This is the whole trick and it saves an hour of pain. Node | Result | StaticBody2D you move in code | The player doesn't ride it. Platform slides out from under them, or squishes them into the ceiling. | CharacterBody2D | Works, but you're re-implementing what the engine already does. | AnimatableBody2D | ✅ Built exactly for this. Moves where you tell it and carries whatever is standing on it. | AnimatableBody2D is a physics body designed to be moved by code or an AnimationPlayer while still pushing other bodies properly. Its Sync to Physics property (on by default) is what makes the player ride along. The platform scene Scene → New Scene → Other Node → AnimatableBody2D, save as . Version A: between two markers (most flexible) In your level scene, add two Marker2Ds — and — and drag them where the platform should travel. walks a value toward a target at a fixed rate and stops exactly there — no overshoot. It's the same function Patrol Enemies uses. The lines give you drag-and-drop slots in the Inspector: drop in PointA and PointB and the platform is configured. Drag one platform scene into a level four times, point each at different markers, and you have four platforms with zero extra code. Parent the markers to the level, not the platform A marker parented to the platform moves with it, so the platform chases a target it can never reach and drifts off screen forever. Version B: no markers, just a distance Fewer moving parts, good for a team in a hurry. Set in the Inspector per instance. makes an elevator; makes a slider. Version C: zero code (AnimationPlayer) Add an AnimationPlayer child, new animation , Loop on, Autoplay on. Key at 0s and 2s at one end, and at 1s at the other end. Set the interpolation curve to Ease In-Out for a smooth glide. Genuinely the best option for a team with a strong artist and a nervous programmer — and it's the option Godot's AnimatableBody2D was designed around. Variations A falling platform — stand on it, it shakes, then drops: Add a thin Area2D just above the platform surface. The shake is a warning — a platform that falls with no telegraph feels unfair. A one-way moving platform — check One Way Collision on the CollisionShape2D so you can jump up through it (CollisionShape2D). A conveyor belt — a StaticBody2D with Physics Material Override → Friction 0, plus a nudge in the player's script while . A crumbling platform — like the falling one, but instead of dropping, with a fade-out tween. A platform on a circular path: Common problems Problem | Fix | Player doesn't move with the platform | It's a StaticBody2D — change it to AnimatableBody2D | Player jitters while riding | Move it in , never . Confirm Sync to Physics is on. | Platform pushes the player into a wall and they vibrate | Give the player a CapsuleShape2D and leave clearance at the end of the run | Platform drifts away forever | Markers parented to the platform instead of the level | Player slides off a horizontal platform | Expected in some engines — AnimatableBody2D handles it. If it persists, check the player is a CharacterBody2D using | Jumping off feels weak | Known platformer quirk: the player doesn't inherit platform momentum. Usually fine; ignore it on Day 4. |

h: The catch: Area2D can't be blocked

b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day Walls, crates, pillars — things the player bumps into instead of dying to. This is the piece that turns an open field into a level. The obstacles that do kill you are Hazards; the full layer system is in CharacterBody2D. The catch: Area2D can't be blocked In Dodge the Creeps the player is an . Areas detect overlaps but have no physical presence — nothing can stop them. Walk straight through your beautiful wall. The fix is to change the player's root node type: 1. Right-click the Player node in the Scene dock → Change Type → . 2. Update the movement script to use the built-in and (below). Everything else about the player — the sprite, the shape, the animations — stays exactly as it is. Step 1: name your collision layers Project → Project Settings → Layer Names → 2D Physics. Naming them once means you never have to remember what "Layer 3" was. Use the camp-wide scheme from Collision Layers and Masks — for this note you only need the first three: 1 player, 2 mobs, 3 obstacles. Step 2: the new player script is built in on — you don't declare it, you just set it. does the moving and the sliding along walls. Don't also set from the input; pick one. Set the player's collision Mask to obstacles only. That way stops you at walls but you don't physically shove the mobs around like bumper cars. Step 3: hit detection moves to a Hurtbox The player no longer detects mobs by itself, so give it a child that does. Add an child named Hurtbox with its own . Set the Hurtbox's Mask to the mobs layer, connect its signal (Signals), and move your death code there: turns the hurtbox off safely — disabling a shape directly in the middle of a collision throws an error. Step 4: the obstacle itself Dead simple, and no script at all: Save as and drag as many copies into your level as you want. It blocks the player because the player's mask includes obstacles. It doesn't kill anyone because it isn't on the mobs layer. Lots of walls? Use a TileMap instead Hand-placing twenty s is slow. In your Main/Level scene (not inside the Goomba!): Markers must NOT be children of the Goomba If the points are inside the enemy, they move with it — the Goomba chases its own feet and moonwalks off the map. Put them in the level, as siblings of the enemy. Empty slots = instant crash on . — returns -1 or 1: "is my target left or right of me?" Same trick as the Camera2D look-ahead. — a 10-pixel "close enough" zone. Never compare positions with . — the swap: whichever point we reached, aim at the other one. — face the walk direction (AnimatedSprite2D). Multiple levels: swap the tilemap, keep everything else
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧩 Mechanics Index · Used on Day 4 - Production Day, Day 5 - Polish and Showcase How to move between screens: Title → Game → Game Over → restart. This is what makes a project feel like a real, finished game. The three screens of a tiny game Each is its own scene (Scenes and Nodes). Switch to another scene means "from the project root." The path must match the file in the FileSystem dock exactly. A title screen with a Start button On , add a , connect its signal (Signals): Or start on any key (good for a one-button game): Restart the current game Simplest restart — reload the scene you're in: Multiple levels: swap the tilemap, keep everything else For games where the "levels" are just different tilemaps — , , each a painted TileMapLayer — and the start and exit are in the same place every level. The player touches the exit, the old tilemap is swapped for the next one, and the player teleports back to the start. Because the player never gets destroyed, score, lives, and power-ups carry over automatically — no autoload needed. The level scenes: each is a scene whose root is a TileMapLayer (TileMapLayer) with the level painted on it. Nothing else in them — no player, no exit. Design rule: every level's path must start and end at the same two spots. The Main scene owns everything permanent: Script on Main — connect the Exit's signal (Signals) to the Main node (in the connect dialog, pick Main instead of Exit): — in the Inspector, set the array size and drag each level's .tscn into a slot. The array order IS the level order — rearranging your game is drag-and-drop, no code. — without it, a player who ran into the exit at full speed keeps that momentum into the next level. — swapping physics objects (the tilemap) during a collision callback makes Godot complain ("flushing queries" error). Deferring waits for the physics step to finish. Needed any time triggers scene surgery. Mask: player on the Exit — a mob wandering into the door won't finish the level (CharacterBody2D). When the array runs out, the win screen loads — that's the one real left in the flow. Testing a specific level Change in to to jump straight to level 3 while testing. Just change it back before the showcase. Go to a game-over screen Quit (optional) Minimum for "looks finished" A title screen with your game's name + team names, and a way to restart. That's the Day 5 polish bar (Day 5 - Polish and Showcase). You don't need a separate game-over scene — reusing the title screen is fine. Carrying the score between scenes When you , the old scene (and its variables) is destroyed, so the score resets. To show the final score on a game-over screen, store it in an autoload/global script — that's Autoload and Global. Only attempt it if your team has time.

Then a leaderboard with names on it. This is the feature that turns showcase night into an actual arcade. A game with a high score table gets played over and over by the same people; a game without one gets played once. Arcade Architects, after all. Where saved files go is a real folder Godot manages per project ( on Windows). Use it for anything you write at runtime. Never save to is your project folder. It's read-only in an exported game, so saving there works while you're testing in the editor and silently fails for everyone at the showcase. Always . The simplest version: one number Use it: The check is the whole trick: the first time anyone plays there's no file, and reading a missing file crashes. A real leaderboard: top 10 with names JSON is just text, so you can open in Notepad and read it — very handy for debugging, and for resetting the board between showcase sessions. with is a lambda — a function written inline. It means "a comes before b when a's score is higher." Displaying the board Use a monospace font on that Label so the columns line up (Label and CanvasLayer). Three-letter initials (the arcade way) Don't use a keyboard text box. Three letters you cycle with up/down is the authentic arcade feel and it's more fun: wraps around, so past Z comes back to A. Saving other things too The same file can hold anything — swap the single value for a dictionary: Store it with and read it back with . That's a complete save system for a small game. 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 2 — Showcase Payoff Difficulty: ⭐ easy · Payoff: ⭐⭐⭐ huge · Time: 10 minutes Backgrounds that scroll slower than the foreground, creating an illusion of depth. Distant mountains drift; nearby bushes rush past. It costs almost nothing and it's the closest thing to a cheat code for making a game look finished. The idea Look out a car window. Fence posts blur past. Mountains barely move. Your brain reads that speed difference as distance. Parallax fakes it in 2D. Setup in Godot 4.3+ Use Parallax2D — one node per layer, no wrapper needed. 1. Add a Parallax2D node to your scene. 2. Add a Sprite2D child and drop your background art in. 3. Set Parallax2D's Scroll Scale — means "move at 20% of camera speed." 4. Repeat for each layer. Rule: farther away = smaller Scroll Scale. is painted on the screen and never moves; moves exactly with the world. Making it repeat forever Set Repeat Size to your image's width (e.g. for a 1920px-wide image) and Godot tiles it endlessly as you scroll. Set only the x for horizontal-scrolling games. For this to look seamless the art must be tileable — the right edge has to line up with the left. Most free parallax packs on itch.io already are; look for "seamless" or "loopable" in the description. Older Godot 4 (ParallaxBackground) If you're on 4.0–4.2, the older pair still works: Same concepts, different property names: Motion Scale = Scroll Scale, Motion Mirroring = Repeat Size. It needs a camera Parallax reacts to a moving Camera2D. In a single-screen game (Pong, Space Invaders, Dodge the Creeps) nothing scrolls, so nothing parallaxes. For those, scroll the background yourself: This is arguably better than real parallax for an arcade game. An endlessly drifting starfield behind a fixed-screen shooter looks fantastic and works with zero camera setup. Choosing layers Three layers is the sweet spot. More is rarely worth the effort. Layer | Scroll Scale | Content | Sky / gradient | 0.0 – 0.1 | flat colour, stars, sun | Far | 0.2 – 0.4 | mountains, city skyline, distant trees | Near | 0.5 – 0.8 | bushes, fences, foreground grass | World | 1.0 | your TileMapLayer | Fade the distance Set far layers' to a slightly washed-out tint ( ). Real distance desaturates and blues things — this is called atmospheric perspective, and it sells depth even harder than the motion does. Common problems Problem | Fix | Background doesn't move at all | No Camera2D, or the camera isn't moving. Use the auto-scroll script instead | Visible seam when it repeats | Art isn't tileable, or Repeat Size doesn't exactly match the image width | Background covers the level | Set the Parallax2D's to a negative number | Layers move the wrong relative amounts | Far layers need smaller scroll scales — it's easy to get backwards | Repeat looks stretched | Don't scale the sprite; set Repeat Size to the scaled width if you must |

🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 2 — Showcase Payoff Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐⭐ high · Time: 20 minutes Explosions, sparks, dust, smoke, magic trails, rain. Juice and Game Feel uses a particle burst for a death effect — this is the full node. GPUParticles2D vs CPUParticles2D Node | Use when | GPUParticles2D | default choice. Thousands of particles, runs on the graphics card | CPUParticles2D | old/weak hardware, or a laptop where GPU particles render as black squares | Same properties, same ideas. If particles look broken on a school laptop, right-click the node → Convert to CPUParticles2D. Keep this in your back pocket for Friday. Setting one up 1. Add a GPUParticles2D node. 2. Inspector → Process Material → → New ParticleProcessMaterial. (Nothing renders until you do this.) 3. Texture → drag in a small image — a white dot, a star, a puff. A 16×16 soft circle covers most needs. 4. Amount → how many particles exist at once. 5. Press play in the viewport to preview. Two empty slots = nothing visible No Process Material, or no Texture, means invisible particles. Godot doesn't warn you. Check both first. The properties that matter Under Process Material: Property | Does | Direction | which way they head. = up | Spread | cone angle in degrees. = every direction | Initial Velocity Min/Max | speed range. Set them apart for natural variety | Gravity | falls, floats up like smoke, drifts | Scale Min/Max | particle size | Color | tint. Use a Gradient to fade out over life | Angular Velocity | spin | Damping | slows particles down over time | On the node itself: Property | Does | Amount | particle count | Lifetime | seconds each particle lives | One Shot | ✅ for a burst, ❌ for a continuous stream | Explosiveness | = steady trickle, = all at once. Set to 1 for explosions | Emitting | on/off switch — the thing you toggle from code | Local Coords | ❌ so particles stay behind when the emitter moves (correct for trails) | The single most important setting Explosiveness = 1 plus One Shot = on is the difference between "an explosion" and "a sad sprinkle." Almost every burst effect wants both. Firing one from code A continuous effect (dust while running, a rocket flame): A one-shot burst (One Shot ✅, Explosiveness ): A burst that outlives the thing that died — the important pattern. A particle child of a node you disappears instantly, so spawn it into the scene instead: Make a GPUParticles2D with One Shot on, and give it this script so it cleans itself up: Recipes Effect | Settings | Explosion | One Shot ✅, Explosiveness 1, Spread 180, Velocity 150–350, Gravity (0, 200), orange→red gradient | Footstep dust | Emitting toggled by movement, Spread 30, Direction (0,-1), low velocity, small scale, brown | Magic sparkle | Gravity (0,0), slow velocity, Angular Velocity high, star texture, Damping 20 | Smoke | Gravity (0,-60), scale grows over life, grey, low Explosiveness, long Lifetime | Rain | Emission Shape → Box across the top, Gravity (0, 900), thin vertical texture | Blood / juice hit | One Shot, Explosiveness 1, Spread 60 aimed away from impact, Gravity on | Jet trail | Local Coords ❌, continuous, Direction opposite to travel | Emission shapes Process Material → Emission Shape controls where particles spawn: Point (default), Sphere (a circular puff), Box (rain, a wall of fire), or Points (an exact custom pattern). Sphere with a small radius makes an explosion read much better than a single point. Where to use them Enemy death (Health and Lives) Coin collection (Collectables) Landing from a jump, running dust (Platformer Physics) Dash trail (Dash and Double Jump) — though the ghost-sprite trick there looks better for a character Bullet impacts (Making Bullets) Lava bubbles, sparks off spikes (Hazards) Ambient snow or falling leaves — instant atmosphere for a whole level Common problems Problem | Fix | Nothing visible | Missing Process Material or Texture | Black squares | Convert to CPUParticles2D — a driver issue on old laptops | Fires only once, never again | Use , not | Particles vanish when the enemy dies | Spawn the effect as a separate scene, don't parent it to the dying node | Trail follows the player in a clump | Uncheck Local Coords | Explosion looks like a fountain | Explosiveness is 0 — set it to 1 | Game slows to a crawl | Amount is in the thousands. 20–50 is plenty for a burst |

h: Godot pauses the whole tree for you
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 2 — Showcase Payoff Difficulty: ⭐ easy · Payoff: ⭐⭐ solid · Time: 15 minutes Press Escape, everything freezes, a menu appears. Small feature, and it's one of the clearest signals that a game is finished rather than a prototype. Builds on Label and CanvasLayer and Scene Switching. Godot pauses the whole tree for you One line stops , , Timers, animations, and input handling across the entire scene tree. Which is the problem — it also freezes your pause menu, so nothing can unpause it. That's the soft-lock every team hits. The fix: Process Modes Every node has Inspector → Process → Mode: Mode | Behaviour | Inherit | same as its parent (the default) | Pausable | stops when paused — the normal game | When Paused | runs only when paused | Always | runs no matter what | Set your pause menu's CanvasLayer to (or ). Now it keeps running while everything else is frozen. The scene The ColorRect behind the panel is the whole visual trick — it separates the menu from the frozen game underneath and takes ten seconds. The script Put this on your Main scene (or on the PauseLayer itself): Connect each Button's signal (Label and CanvasLayer). Unpause before you change scenes is not reset by loading a new scene. Forget the line and your restarted game loads permanently frozen, with no menu to unpause it. This is the single most common bug in this note. Use , not only fires if no UI element already consumed the event, so a focused Button won't swallow your Escape key. It's the right choice for any global hotkey. Nice additions Fade the dim panel in (Tweens) instead of snapping: Tweens need on the node running them, or they freeze too. Duck the music while paused (AudioStreamPlayer): Pause automatically when the window loses focus — genuinely useful at a showcase when someone walks away mid-game: Keyboard/controller navigation: click the Resume button → Inspector → Focus → Neighbour Top/Bottom to link the buttons, and call when the menu opens. Now the menu works on a gamepad (Two-Player and Gamepad). Also useful for Same Process Mode trick, different content: A game over overlay that freezes the action behind it A level complete screen with a score tally A cutscene or dialogue box that pauses gameplay (Dialogue and Text Boxes) A settings panel — volume sliders, fullscreen toggle Common problems Problem | Fix | Menu appears but nothing responds | PauseLayer's Process Mode isn't Always | Restarted game is frozen forever | Missing before the scene change | Escape does nothing | Using and a Button is eating it — use | Menu shows but the game keeps running | You showed the menu without setting | Pause fade animation is frozen | The tweening node also needs Process Mode Always | Menu is behind the game | It's not under a CanvasLayer |

h: The core idea: one scene, exported action names
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 2 — Showcase Payoff Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐⭐ huge (on Friday) · Time: 20 minutes Two people playing at once, and controller support. Bouncing Ball builds a two-player Pong; this is the general technique for any game. Why bother At a showcase, a two-player game draws a crowd and a single-player game draws a line. People wait their turn for one and gather around the other. If a team is undecided about their pitch on Day 3, this is a strong argument for versus or co-op. The core idea: one scene, exported action names Don't build and . Build one player scene whose input action names are ed, then set them per instance in the Inspector. Drag the scene in twice, change five strings on the second one, done. One script to fix bugs in, two players. Setting up the Input Map Project → Project Settings → Input Map. Create both sets: Player 1 | Keys | Player 2 | Keys | | W | | ↑ | | S | | ↓ | | A | | ← | | D | | → | | Space | | Enter | Sit them apart WASD and the arrow keys are far enough apart that two people can share one keyboard without fighting for elbow room. Don't put both players on the same half. Adding controllers An action can hold several events at once — keyboard and gamepad. In the Input Map, click + next to an action and choose Joypad Button or Joypad Axis. The key field is Device: Device 0 = first controller, Device 1 = second, and so on. Device -1 / "All Devices" = any controller. Fine for single-player, wrong for two-player — both players would move on either pad. So for real two-player controller support: actions get gamepad events on Device 0, actions get the same buttons on Device 1. Analog sticks already returns analog values, so a stick gives you smooth 0–1 movement for free. Add Joypad Axis → Left Stick events to your directional actions and it just works. Deadzone (a field on each action, default ) stops a worn stick from drifting. Raise it to if a controller creeps on its own. Detecting connected controllers Swapping the button prompts on screen when a player picks up a controller is a small touch that reads as very polished. Godot also emits a signal when a pad is plugged in mid-game: Rumble Fire it when the player takes damage (Health and Lives) or lands a hit. Costs one line and feels great — see Juice and Game Feel. Co-op vs versus Versus is easier to design and better at a showcase. Pong, a shooting duel, a race, a king-of-the-hill. Scoring is obvious and matches end quickly, so the queue moves. Co-op needs more thought — a shared Camera2D has to frame both players. The cheap fix is a fixed camera on one screen; the real fix is a camera that follows the midpoint and zooms out as they separate: Simplest co-op of all: keep both players on one screen and don't let them leave it. Clamp their positions to the viewport and skip cameras entirely. Common problems Problem | Fix | Both players move together | Both instances still use — set the exports on player 2 | Both pads control both players | Device is (All Devices). Set 0 and 1 explicitly | Controller does nothing | Plug it in before launching; check | Character drifts on its own | Raise the action's deadzone | Keys "stick" with 3+ pressed at once | Cheap keyboards have limited rollover — this is hardware, not code. Use controllers | Player 2 falls off screen in co-op | Clamp positions, or use the midpoint camera |

h: Writing dialogue in a separate file
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 3 — Genre Unlocks Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐⭐ high · Time: 45 minutes A character speaks, text types out one letter at a time, you press a key to continue. This unlocks narrative games — and for Girls Who Game specifically, it's the bridge from the Twine work students already know how to design to the engine they're learning this week. You already know how to write these If you've made a Twine game, you've written branching dialogue. This note is only about displaying it in Godot. The hard part — writing something worth reading — you've already practised. The dialogue box scene Scene → New Scene → CanvasLayer, save as . Use a RichTextLabel, not a Label — it supports , , and shaky text, and it wraps properly. Check Fit Content and turn on BBCode Enabled. The typewriter effect Text appearing one character at a time is the whole feel of dialogue. It's five lines. is the trick — a RichTextLabel property from 0 to 1 controlling how much of the text is shown. Tween it and you have a typewriter with no per-character loop (Tweens). Set the CanvasLayer's Process Mode to Always or the tween freezes with the paused game (Pause Menu). Advancing, and skipping The skip-on-first-press behaviour is not optional. Players who read faster than 40 characters a second will mash the key, and without it they'll blow straight past three lines of your story. Triggering it An Area2D the player walks into, or an interact press near an NPC: gives you a proper multi-line text box in the Inspector — the writer on the team can edit dialogue without opening a script. That's the single most useful line in this note for a mixed-skill team. Make the dialogue box an autoload so any scene can call it. Writing dialogue in a separate file Once you have more than a few conversations, put them in JSON instead of scattering them across scenes. Create : Now the whole script of your game lives in one readable file. from anywhere. This is how real narrative games do it — reading from is fine because you never write to it (High Scores That Persist explains why writing there fails). Branching choices (the Twine part) naming another key in the JSON is exactly a Twine passage link. Put the Buttons in a VBoxContainer so they arrange themselves (Label and CanvasLayer). Polish that matters A blip sound per character. Play a short click every few letters — it's the difference between text and a character talking. Keep it quiet and vary slightly. A portrait that changes with the speaker. One , swap the texture per line. BBCode for emphasis: RichTextLabel animates it for free. Blink the ▼ indicator with a looping tween so players know to press something. Patrol Enemies and Homing Enemies are the two halves; this is the note that joins them into something that feels alive. The idea An enemy is in exactly one state at a time, and each state has its own behaviour and its own rules for switching. That's it — no framework required, just an and a . The whole thing creates named numbers — instead of . is GDScript's switch: it runs only the branch that matches. is where "entry actions" go — the alert sound plays once when the chase begins, not sixty times a second. The states Seeing the player The simplest version — an Area2D "aggro zone" child: A better version that can't see through walls uses a RayCast2D — that note covers vision cones and line-of-sight properly. Making states end and need to finish and hand control back: Connect AnimationPlayer's signal, or use a Timer — either works. This unlocks puzzle games — Sokoban, Bomberman, Snake, roguelikes, Pokémon-style overworlds. The best genre for a 5-day camp Puzzle games are finishable. There's no game feel to tune, no enemy AI to balance, no juice required — a puzzle either works or it doesn't. A team that builds ten good Sokoban levels ships a complete game. A team building a platformer ships one level and a wish list. If a team is anxious about scope on Day 3, point them here. The core idea The player has a grid position ( = column 3, row 5) which is the truth, and a pixel position that animates to catch up. Movement is a series of discrete, validated steps — not continuous physics. Use (integer vectors) for grid coordinates and for pixels. Keeping them separate prevents a whole category of rounding bugs. The guard makes movement feel deliberate and stops inputs queuing into a slide. Checking what's walkable with a TileMapLayer returns for an empty cell, so "no wall tile here" means you can walk. Drag your wall TileMapLayer into the export slot. Set the TileMapLayer's tile size to match . Sokoban: pushing boxes The genre-defining mechanic, and it's about fifteen lines. And on the box: Win when every box is on a goal tile: Undo (do this — it's what makes a puzzle game playable) A puzzle game without undo is a puzzle game where every mistake means restarting. h: The idea: a hitbox that turns on briefly
The three things that make melee feel good
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 3 — Genre Unlocks Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐⭐ high · Time: 40 minutes A sword swing, a punch, a spear jab. Making Bullets covers shooting; this covers hitting things that are right in front of you — which is what roughly half of teams actually want. The idea: a hitbox that turns on briefly A melee attack is an Area2D that is off most of the time and on for a fraction of a second. Everything else is timing and feel. Hitbox = deals damage. Hurtbox = receives it. Keep the words straight and the rest follows (Collision Layers and Masks). The SwordPivot is a plain Node2D with the Hitbox offset to the right of it. Rotate the pivot and the whole swing arc rotates with it — the same trick as the orbiting spike ball. The attack script Add to Project Settings → Input Map (J, Z, or left mouse are all fine), and an Timer (One Shot ✅, Wait Time ). is cleaner than disabling the shape — no needed (Area2D). Dealing the damage Connect the Hitbox's (or if your enemies use hurtboxes): means the same sword hurts enemies, breakable crates, and boss weak points without any special cases (Health and Lives). The three things that make melee feel good Melee lives or dies on feedback. A sword that silently deletes an enemy feels like nothing. These three take about ten minutes total and they're the whole difference. 1. Knockback — shove the target away: On the enemy: 2. Hit-stop — freeze the whole game for a few frames on impact. This is the secret ingredient in every game that feels good to hit things in: The flags make the timer ignore , so it isn't slowed by the very slowdown it's timing. Sixty milliseconds is invisible as a pause and enormous as a feeling. 3. A flash and a sound. The enemy flashes white, a sound plays. Both are in Juice and Game Feel. Add a little Camera2D shake on a heavy hit. Better timing with AnimationPlayer The version above uses a fixed . Better: let the animation decide exactly when the blade is dangerous, using Call Method tracks (AnimationPlayer): Now the designer tunes the attack by dragging keyframes — wind-up, active frames, recovery — instead of guessing at numbers. This is how fighting games are built. Variations Charge attack — hold to charge, release for more damage: Combo — chain up to three swings if you press again during the recovery window. Track , reset it with a Timer. Spin attack — rotate the pivot a full and leave the hitbox on for the whole rotation. Stomp (jump on their head) — no hitbox needed; already covered in Patrol Enemies. Enemy melee — the mirror image: an enemy hitbox masking player, telegraphed by a wind-up animation. Always telegraph. An enemy that attacks instantly is unfair; one that raises its arm for 0.4 seconds first is a fight. 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 3 — Genre Unlocks Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐ solid · Time: 30 minutes Asteroids movement: you rotate, you thrust forward, you drift, and you wrap around the screen edges. It's a completely different feel from the eight-directional movement in Movement and Input — and it's the single most arcade control scheme there is. Arcade Architects, after all. If a team wants to build something that feels like it belongs in a cabinet, this is it. Rotate-and-thrust movement The key difference: the direction you face and the direction you're travelling are not the same thing. That gap is the entire skill of the genre. is the ship's facing direction as a unit vector. This assumes your sprite's nose points right at rotation 0 — draw it that way, or add to correct art that points up. Adding to velocity rather than setting it is what creates momentum. You can be facing forward and still sliding backward, which is the whole game. gives you true frictionless space — authentic, and much harder. Start around and let playtesters decide (Playtesting). is a particle emitter on the back of the ship. One line, and thrusting reads. Screen wrap Fly off the left edge, appear on the right. Or the one-liner version: wraps a float into a range — the same helper used for cycling letters in High Scores That Persist. The pop-in problem The ship vanishes at one edge and appears at the other with nothing in between, which looks abrupt. The proper arcade fix is to draw a second copy of the ship near the opposite edge while it's straddling the boundary. It's fiddly. The cheap fix that's almost as good: wrap based on the sprite's centre but let it travel half a sprite-width past the edge before wrapping, so it exits fully before reappearing. Shooting forward Bullets inherit the ship's facing, not the ship's velocity (Making Bullets): Give the bullet the same and it circles the screen too — which is very Asteroids, and occasionally lets you shoot yourself in the back. That's a feature. Splitting asteroids The genre's other signature mechanic. One asteroid scene, an exported size, and it spawns smaller copies of itself when destroyed: A scene that instantiates itself is a genuinely lovely idea to show students — one scene file produces the entire cascade of an asteroid field breaking apart. is a full circle in radians (2π), which is nicer than typing . Draw it pointing right or subtract | Impossible to control | is authentic and brutal. Raise it, or lower | Ship spins wildly | too high — 3–4 rad/s is comfortable | Wrapping flickers at the edge | Wrapping every frame while sitting exactly on the boundary. A torch in a cave, a flashlight beam, a spooky night level, a glowing pickup. Enormous mood change for about fifteen minutes of work. The two-node trick Lighting in 2D Godot is basically one idea: 1. CanvasModulate — tints the entire scene. Set it dark. Now it's night. 2. PointLight2D — adds light back in specific places. That's it. Two nodes, and a bright level becomes a cave. Never use pure black makes unlit areas totally invisible and unplayable. Dark blue or dark purple reads as night while letting players still see shapes. Real night isn't black either. PointLight2D It needs a texture. A PointLight2D with an empty Texture slot does nothing — this is the #1 mistake here, same shape as the empty-shape problem in CollisionShape2D. Use a soft white radial gradient (a blurry white circle on transparent). Grab one from Asset Resources, or make one in seconds: add a , set Fill to Radial, and make the gradient run white → transparent. Property | Does | Texture | the light's shape. Required | Texture Scale | how big the light is | Color | light colour — warm orange for fire, pale blue for moonlight | Energy | brightness. Above blows out to white | Blend Mode | Add (normal light), Subtract (darkness), Mix | Shadow → Enabled | lets objects cast shadows | A flickering torch is three lines (Tweens): Or add slight randomness per frame for a real fire feel: Shadows 1. On the PointLight2D: Shadow → Enabled ✅. 2. On anything that should block light: add a LightOccluder2D child. 3. Give the occluder an Occluder Polygon and draw the outline. For a TileMapLayer, you can set occlusion per-tile in the TileSet editor (Occlusion Layers) — paint your walls and shadows just work. Shadows are expensive and fiddly. Skip them unless a team specifically wants a stealth or horror game. Lights without shadows already look great. A flashlight cone Use a cone-shaped texture instead of a circle, and rotate the light to face the aim direction: With shadows enabled and a RayCast2D vision check on the enemies, that's a stealth game. Day/night cycle Making things glow A UI or sprite can glow without any lighting setup: 1. Add a WorldEnvironment node. 2. Environment → New Environment → Glow → Enabled ✅. 3. Set Glow HDR Threshold around . 4. Anything brighter than that threshold blooms. Then push a sprite's above 1: . It now glows. Great for Collectables, neon, and lasers. Renderer matters Glow needs Forward+ or Mobile, not Compatibility. Day 1 sets up Compatibility for school laptops, so glow may be unavailable. Lights and CanvasModulate work in all three — glow is the one to check. b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 4 — Worth Knowing Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐ solid · Time: 20 minutes Draw a curve in the editor, and make something travel along it. Enemies that swoop in arcs, patrolling guards on a route, a saw blade circling a room, spawn points around the screen edge. If you've done Day 1, you've already used one — Dodge the Creeps spawns mobs using a Path2D around the screen border. The two nodes Path2D — holds the curve you draw. Does nothing by itself. PathFollow2D — a child of Path2D. Anything parented to it gets dragged along the curve. Drawing a curve 1. Add a Path2D node. 2. In the 2D toolbar, click the ✏️ pencil ("Add Point"). 3. Click in the viewport to place points. 4. Drag while placing to create curve handles instead of sharp corners. 5. Existing point: drag to move, right-click to delete. Press Esc to leave draw mode. Click the Close Curve button in the toolbar for a loop (a circling saw, a racetrack). Moving along it — how far along in pixels. — the same thing from to . Easier for tweening. Two Inspector checkboxes matter: Loop — wraps back to the start at the end. On by default. Rotates — the follower turns to face along the curve. Great for a plane or a car; turn it off for something that should stay upright. Tween along it instead (Tweens) for a swoop with easing: What people actually use it for Swooping enemies (Galaga). The signature move of the genre — enemies fly in along an arc, then take formation. Combine with Enemy Formations: Spawning around the screen edge — the Day 1 pattern: One random number gives you a random point anywhere on the border. Much tidier than four branches for four edges. h: What people actually use it for
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 4 — Worth Knowing Difficulty: ⭐⭐ moderate · Payoff: ⭐⭐ solid · Time: 20 minutes An invisible laser pointer that reports the first thing it hits. Used for ground checks, ledge detection, line of sight, vision cones, and hitscan weapons. Setup Add a RayCast2D child. Two properties matter: Target Position — where the ray points, relative to the node. points 40px down. You can see the line in the editor. Enabled — must be checked, or it does nothing. Set its collision mask to what it should notice (Collision Layers and Masks). Reading it Rays update once per physics frame If you move or rotate a ray and check it in the same frame, you get the old answer. Call first. What people actually use it for Ledge detection — an enemy that doesn't walk off cliffs. The single most useful raycast in a platformer. Point a ray down, just in front of the enemy's feet: Upgrade this straight into Patrol Enemies — it's the difference between a Goomba and a Goomba that keeps falling in the pit. Line of sight — an enemy that can't see through walls. Fixes the main weakness of Enemy States: Set the ray's mask to obstacles and player, so whichever comes first tells you the truth. A vision cone (stealth games). Three or five rays fanned out, plus an angle check: A hitscan weapon — a laser that hits instantly, no bullet to travel: Pairs with Line2D for the visible beam. Wall-jump detection — a ray each side; if it's colliding and you're not on the floor, you can wall-jump (Dash and Double Jump). "Press E to open" — a short forward ray finds the nearest interactable, better than an Area2D when you want the one you're facing (Doors and Keys). ShapeCast2D A ShapeCast2D is the same idea with a whole shape instead of a line, and it can report several hits. Use it when a thin ray keeps slipping past small objects. h: Centered, and why your art is offset
Pixel art settings (do this once, it matters)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 4 — Worth Knowing Difficulty: ⭐ easy · Payoff: ⭐⭐ solid · Time: 10 minutes Shows a picture. It's the most-used node in any 2D game and the core reference never gives it its own page — AnimatedSprite2D covers animation, and this covers the still image underneath. Setup Add a Sprite2D, then drag an image from the FileSystem dock into the Inspector's Texture slot. Done. Even faster: drag the image straight from the FileSystem dock into the 2D viewport and Godot creates the Sprite2D for you. The properties worth knowing Property | Does | Texture | the image | Centered | ✅ (default) origin is the middle; ❌ origin is the top-left | Offset | nudge the art without moving the node | Flip H / Flip V | mirror it — this is how a character turns around | Modulate | tint. to flash, alpha to fade | Region | show only part of the image | Z Index | draw order; higher draws on top | The three you'll use constantly Flipping to face the way you're moving: Two lines, and your character stops moonwalking. Note the guard — without it the sprite snaps back to facing right whenever you stop. Flashing when hit (Health and Lives): Fading out (Tweens): Centered, and why your art is offset Centered is on by default, so the node's position is the middle of the image. For a character standing on the ground it's often nicer to have the origin at their feet — then is where they're standing, and scaling or flipping happens around the right spot. Rather than unchecking Centered, set Offset to (half the sprite height). The origin moves to the feet without changing how anything else works. This is the fix for "my collision shape doesn't line up with my sprite." Pixel art settings (do this once, it matters) Pixel art looks blurry in Godot by default. Two fixes: Per-project (recommended): Project → Project Settings → Rendering → Textures → Default Texture Filter → Nearest. Every sprite in the project is now crisp. Per-texture: select the image in the FileSystem dock → Import tab → Filter off → Reimport. Also set Project Settings → Display → Window → Stretch → Mode: and Aspect: so the game scales cleanly to any window size — important for a projector on showcase day (Exporting Your Game). Region: one image, many sprites Check Region → Enabled and set the Region Rect to show only a slice of a bigger image. Useful when your art came as one packed sheet and you want a single tile from it without cutting the file up. For animation from a sheet, use Hframes / Vframes instead — tell the Sprite2D how many columns and rows the sheet has, then pick with : That's a manual, no-resource way to swap art — handy for a tile variant or a damaged state. Sprite2D vs AnimatedSprite2D Use | When | Sprite2D | a still image, or one you change occasionally in code | AnimatedSprite2D | frame-by-frame animation — walk cycles, idle loops | AnimationPlayer | animating properties (position, rotation, modulate) rather than frames | A Sprite2D plus a couple of Tweens handles a surprising amount of "animation" without any frames at all — squash on landing, spin on death, pulse on pickup. Common problems Problem | Fix | Pixel art is blurry | Set Default Texture Filter to Nearest | Sprite doesn't line up with the collision shape | Use Offset, not by moving the node | Character faces the wrong way | logic inverted, or art drawn facing left | Sprite disappears behind the tilemap | Raise Z Index | Stays red after a hit flash | The never finished, or the reset line got skipped | Whole image shows when you wanted one tile | Region → Enabled unchecked |

h: What people actually use it for
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 4 — Worth Knowing Difficulty: ⭐ easy · Payoff: ⭐⭐ solid · Time: 10 minutes Tells you when something enters or leaves the screen. Small node, and it quietly solves the most common performance bug in a camp game: bullets that never die. The problem it solves Every bullet you fire in Making Bullets flies off screen and keeps existing forever. Fire for two minutes and you have a thousand invisible bullets, each running every frame. The game slows down and nobody can see why. Setup Add a VisibleOnScreenNotifier2D as a child. Size its rectangle in the viewport to roughly cover the sprite. Then connect one of two signals: — became visible — left the view One node, one signal, one line. Add it to your bullet scene and the problem is gone permanently. What people actually use it for Cleaning up bullets — as above. Do this on every bullet scene (Making Bullets). Removing off-screen enemies — a mob that drifted away and is never coming back (Spawning and Timers): Don't free things that start off screen An enemy spawned outside the view fires immediately — or never fires — and deletes itself before it ever arrives. Guard it: Waking enemies only when visible — a big level with fifty enemies runs badly if all fifty are thinking at once: This is the classic optimization for a large TileMapLayer level. Combine with Enemy States so an enemy resumes patrolling where it left off. Keeping the player on screen — flip an enemy or wrap a ship at the boundary (Screen Wrap and Thrust). Triggering a boss or a checkpoint when the player scrolls it into view — a nicer trigger than an Area2D because it reacts to the camera, not to touch. Pausing off-screen Particles to save frames: Checking without a signal VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D — the no-code version There's a sibling node, VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D, that automatically switches its parent's process mode on and off based on visibility. Set Enable Node Path to the node you want managed, and you get the wake-when-visible behaviour with zero script. Use the Enabler when you just want the optimization; use the Notifier when you want to do something specific. Common problems Problem | Fix | Signal never fires | The notifier's rectangle is tiny or zero-sized — size it in the viewport | Enemies vanish before appearing | They spawned off screen. Use the guard | Bullets still pile up | Signal connected on the wrong node, or connected to nothing | Works in the editor, not in game | Rectangle is positioned away from the sprite — check its offset | "Screen" seems wrong | It means the camera's view, not the window. A zoomed-out Camera2D sees more |

h: If they want the co-op feeling
If a student is determined, after camp
What to say in the moment
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 5 — After Camp Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ very hard · Camp verdict: ❌ definitely not · Do instead: Two-Player and Gamepad What it is Two people on two different computers playing the same game together. Godot has real support for it — , , RPCs — and it works. Why definitely not Networking is the hardest thing in this reference by a wide margin, and it's hard in a way that doesn't shrink for small games: Two computers disagree about reality. Every problem downstream comes from this. Latency. Your input arrives 80ms late. Do you rewind time and replay? Real games do. Authority. Who decides whether the shot hit? If it's the shooter, players can cheat. If it's the server, shooting feels laggy. Debugging requires two running games, two sets of logs, and bugs that only appear under real network delay. School networks block things. Firewalls, client isolation on guest wifi, no port forwarding. You can lose a day to infrastructure you don't control before writing a line of game code. Professional teams staff specialists for this. It is not a five-day-camp topic and it's not a "stretch goal" — it's a different discipline. The thing they actually want Almost always: "I want to play with my friend." That's Two-Player and Gamepad, and it's better for a camp. Two players on one keyboard or two controllers, one screen, twenty minutes of work. At the showcase, local multiplayer draws a crowd around the table in a way netplay never could — the fun of two people elbowing each other is the point. | Local (same screen) | Networked | Setup | 20 minutes | days | Debugging | watch the screen | two logs and a packet capture | Works on school wifi | always | often not | Good at a showcase | ✅ a crowd forms | ❌ needs two setups | If they want the co-op feeling Shared-screen co-op — both players in one camera. Two-Player and Gamepad has the midpoint-camera code. Asymmetric co-op — one drives, one shoots. Genuinely interesting design, zero networking. Hot-seat — alternate turns on one machine. Perfect for Grid-Based Movement puzzle and strategy games. Async competition — a shared leaderboard. Players compete without ever being online at the same time, and this is what most arcade "multiplayer" actually was. That last one is worth emphasizing: the original arcade multiplayer was a high score table. You never met the person who set it. You just wanted to beat them. If a student is determined, after camp Godot docs → High-level multiplayer — start here, it's good The / nodes handle a lot automatically Steam and Nakama both offer easier hosting than raw IP connections Advise building a complete single-player game first, then adding networking to it. Learning networking and game design at once is two hard things at once. What to say in the moment "You want to play with your friend, right? Let's put you both on one screen — it's twenty minutes instead of a week, and honestly it's more fun at the showcase because you're sitting next to each other. Online play is a summer-long project; I can point you at where to start if you want it."

h: Why it's usually not worth it in five days
If a student wants it after camp
What to say in the moment
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 5 — After Camp Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐ hard-ish · Camp verdict: ⚠️ rarely worth it · Do instead: Homing Enemies, Enemy States, RayCast2D What it is An enemy that finds its way around walls to reach you, instead of walking straight at you and getting stuck on a corner. Godot provides NavigationRegion2D (the walkable area) and NavigationAgent2D (the thing that follows a computed path). Why it's usually not worth it in five days It's not conceptually hard — it's fiddly. You have to bake a navigation mesh, keep it in sync with your TileMapLayer whenever the level changes, and get the agent's radius and avoidance settings right or enemies jitter, hug walls, or refuse to move. Every one of those is a debugging session, and the failure mode is a silent "enemy stands still." The real question is whether your game needs it. In a single-screen arcade game — which is most camp games — a straight-line chaser is not just adequate, it's correct. Pac-Man's ghosts use hand-written rules, not pathfinding. Cheaper answers that usually work Situation | Do this | Open arena, few walls | Homing Enemies — steer straight at the player | Enemy snags on corners | Add a RayCast2D ahead; if blocked, slide along the wall | Platformer enemy | Patrol Enemies + a ledge raycast. Enemies rarely need to reach you | Grid/puzzle game | Step one tile toward the player — Grid-Based Movement has this in five lines | Enemy should lose you | Enemy States with a give-up distance — often reads smarter than perfect tracking | The "slide along the wall when blocked" trick covers most of what people want pathfinding for: Perfect tracking isn't fun An enemy that always finds the optimal route is harder to escape but usually less enjoyable to play against. Predictable, readable enemy movement is better design for a small game. This is a real design point, not just a scope excuse. If a student wants it after camp Genuinely a good next-step project, and much more pleasant when you're not on a deadline. 1. Add a NavigationRegion2D, draw or bake the walkable polygon. 2. Add a NavigationAgent2D to the enemy. 3. Each frame: , then move toward . Godot docs → Navigation (2D section) Search for baking nav from tiles For a grid game, look up A\ and Godot's built-in — genuinely approachable, and a great introduction to real algorithms What to say in the moment "What's the enemy actually doing wrong? If it's getting stuck on one corner, that's a two-line raycast fix. Full pathfinding is a whole system, and honestly an enemy that's a bit dumb is usually more fun to play against than one that never makes a mistake."

h: If someone goes further after camp
What to say in the moment
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 5 — After Camp Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ hard · Camp verdict: ❌ don't · Do instead: High Scores That Persist What it is Saving the whole game state — where the player is standing, which enemies are dead, which chests are open, inventory contents, quest progress — and restoring it exactly on load. Save slots, autosaves, "continue where you left off." Why not this week The file writing is easy — High Scores That Persist shows the whole technique in about fifteen lines, and it's the same and JSON either way. The hard part isn't saving. It's deciding what counts as "the state of the game." Every object needs to describe itself as data and rebuild itself from that data. Every new feature added on Thursday needs a save/load path too, or loading silently breaks. It's an architectural commitment made on day one, and camp games are built by improvisation — which is the correct way to build them in five days. There's also no need. A tiny game is 3–10 minutes long. Nobody needs to save halfway through, and a save system solves a problem your game doesn't have. What to build instead The want | The five-minute version | "I want progress to persist" | High Scores That Persist — a high score is progress | "I want to unlock levels" | Save one number, , in your Autoload and Global | "I want to keep my settings" | Same file, a dictionary with volume and difficulty | "I want to continue where I left off" | Save the level number only, and restart that level from the beginning | That last row is the good compromise. Saving "you were on level 4" is 95% of the feeling of a save system for 5% of the work, and plenty of real arcade and mobile games do exactly that. Genuinely, that's enough for almost any small game. If someone goes further after camp The standard Godot approach: give every saveable node a method returning a dictionary and a method that restores it, put them all in a group, and iterate. Godot docs → Saving games Look up for the -based approach, which is cleaner Warn them about with objects — it can execute arbitrary code on load and is a real security issue in a shared game. JSON is safer. What to say in the moment "Writing the file is easy — you already know how from the high score note. The hard part is describing your whole game as data, and that's a design decision you'd have to make before you started building. How about we save which level you reached? That's most of the feeling, and it's ten minutes."

h: The exception: copy-paste a hit flash
Where to send a curious student
What to say in the moment
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 5 — After Camp Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ hard · Camp verdict: ⚠️ copy-paste only · Do instead: Tweens, Particles, Lights and CanvasModulate What it is Small programs that run on the graphics card, once per pixel. They're how you get a white flash on hit, water ripples, dissolve effects, outlines, screen distortion, and CRT scanlines. Written in a separate language (Godot Shading Language, close to GLSL), with its own math and its own mental model. Why not this week Shaders are a whole second language on top of GDScript, and the debugging story is bad — a mistake usually produces a blank screen or a pink rectangle rather than an error message pointing at a line. A student who's still getting comfortable with statements will not have a good time. The bigger issue is opportunity cost. Almost everything a camp game wants from a shader has a non-shader answer that takes five minutes: for a tint flash, Particles for effects, Lights and CanvasModulate for mood, Tweens for motion. The exception: copy-paste a hit flash If a team wants the white-flash-on-hit effect specifically, hand them this. Don't teach it — hand it over. Create a new Shader resource on the sprite's Material slot: This looks noticeably better than because it preserves the sprite's silhouette instead of washing it out. It's the one shader worth the trouble in a camp game — great for Melee Attacks and Health and Lives. Where to send a curious student godotshaders.com — a large library of free, ready-to-paste shaders. Genuinely the best resource, and using someone else's shader is a legitimate skill. The Book of Shaders (thebookofshaders.com) — the classic gentle introduction, though it's not Godot-specific. Godot docs → Shading section. Encourage using shaders from the library now, and writing them later. Downloading a water shader and tweaking its parameters is a real, satisfying skill that requires none of the math. What to say in the moment "You can absolutely use shaders — grab one from godotshaders.com and change the numbers. Writing your own is a summer project; it's a whole second language and the error messages are unhelpful. What effect are you actually going for? There's probably a five-minute version."

h: If a student really wants it
What to say in the moment
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · 🧰 Extras Index · 📁 Tier 5 — After Camp Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ hard · Camp verdict: ❌ don't · Do instead: Enemy States What it is A formal architecture where every behaviour — Idle, Walk, Jump, Attack, Hurt — is its own node with its own script, and a manager node hands control between them. Godot also ships AnimationTree with a built-in state machine for blending animations. It's the standard way large games structure characters, and it's genuinely good engineering. Why not this week You already have a state machine. The + pattern in Enemy States is one — it just doesn't have a folder of files around it. The formal version pays off when you have a dozen states, several characters sharing behaviour, and months to maintain it. In five days it costs you a day of setup and buys nothing a statement doesn't already do. Teams that go down this road on Wednesday are still debugging their state manager on Friday instead of making levels. AnimationTree is worse for camp purposes: the blend-space UI is genuinely confusing, and students find it in the docs and assume it's required. It isn't. The honest comparison | statement (Enemy States) | Formal state machine | Setup time | 0 minutes | 1–2 hours | Adding a state | 3 lines | a new script and node | Readable at a glance | ✅ one function shows everything | ❌ spread across files | Scales past 10 states | ❌ gets long | ✅ stays clean | Right for a 5-day camp | ✅ | ❌ | If a student really wants it They probably don't need talking out of it so much as timing advice: this is a great first project after camp, when they have a game that already works and want to refactor it. Point them at: Godot docs → AnimationTree and StateMachine guides The community "Finite State Machine" tutorials — search Their own Enemy States enemy as the thing to refactor. Refactoring code you wrote and understand is the best possible way to learn an architecture pattern. What to say in the moment "You already built a state machine — the block is the machine. The fancier version splits it into files, which helps when you have twenty states. You have four. Build the game this week; refactor it in July if you still want to."
