h: Flavor constraints (optional — draw one for spice)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 3 - Design Day · 🖨️ Print & cut into cards. Constraints spark ideas (see Tiny Game Design). On Day 3, each team draws one core constraint (required) and may draw one flavor constraint (optional spice). Every game must also obey The Tiny Game Rules. Core constraints (draw one — required) # | Constraint | Means | 1 | One screen | The whole game fits on one screen. No scrolling. | 2 | One button | The entire game is played with a single key. | 3 | One mechanic | The player can really only do one kind of action. | 4 | No movement | The player can't move — the world moves around them. | 5 | You can't win | The goal is to last as long as possible (high score). | 6 | Two colors only | The whole game uses just two colors. | Flavor constraints (optional — draw one for spice) # | Flavor | Means | A | Roles reversed | The "enemy" is the goal; the "goal" hurts you. | B | It speeds up | The game gets faster the longer you survive. | C | One life | One mistake and it's over. | D | Everything falls | Gravity rules; things drop from the top. | E | Silent → loud | Starts calm, ends chaotic. | F | Tiny hero, big world | You're small; everything else is huge. | How to use a constraint 1. Draw your core card. Read it aloud to your team. 2. Brainstorm: "What game could we make where [constraint]?" 3. Don't fight the constraint — use it. "One button" isn't a problem to solve; it's the whole personality of your game (Flappy Bird is one button). 4. Turn the best idea into a One-Sentence Pitch. Constraint → idea One button + everything falls → "You're a bucket; tap to dash left/right and catch falling eggs before they smash." No movement + you can't win → "You're a lighthouse; rotate your beam to keep boats off the rocks as long as you can."

h: NOT in the MVP (this is Day 5 polish)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 4 - Production Day, Day 5 - Polish and Showcase · 🖨️ Print one per team; tape to the monitor. MVP = Minimum Viable Product — the smallest version of your game someone can actually play. On Day 4 you build to this list and nothing more. Polish is Day 5. The MVP bar (all four = playable) [ ] Start — the game begins (a key, a button, or it just runs) [ ] Core loop works — the player can do the main action (Tiny Game Design) [ ] Win or lose — there's a clear end (you survived / you crashed / you scored enough) [ ] Restart — the player can play again without quitting (Scene Switching) If a stranger can sit down, play, reach a win or loss, and go again without you explaining — you have an MVP. That's the whole Day 4 goal. Your team's build list (fill in) Write the 3–5 specific pieces your game needs. Example for a coin-catcher: [ ] Player moves left/right (Movement and Input) [ ] Coins fall from the top (Spawning and Timers) [ ] Catching a coin adds score (Area2D + Score and UI) [ ] Miss 3 coins = game over (Scene Switching) [ ] Press a key to restart Your list: [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] NOT in the MVP (this is Day 5 polish) Multiple levels · fancy art · particles · screen shake · menus beyond a title · story · extra enemy types. Cross these out of your brain until the MVP is done. (Day 5 - Polish and Showcase) Day 4 scope cut At end of day, cross off anything you won't finish by Friday 3 PM. Get an instructor signature. After today: no new features, polish only. The trap "It would be so cool if it also had ." Maybe! Write it on a "someday" list and keep building the MVP. Cool unfinished games don't get shown Friday; finished simple ones do (The Tiny Game Rules).

🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 5 - Polish and Showcase · 🖨️ Print as a fill-in slip. If your team can't say your game in one sentence, it's too big (The Tiny Game Rules). Writing the sentence is the design decision. Lock it on Day 3 and get it instructor-approved. The template You are a who until . First blank: who/what you are (the character) Second blank: what you do — the core loop verb (Tiny Game Design) Third blank: how it ends — the win or lose condition Examples "You are a raccoon who stacks trash higher and higher until it topples." "You are one firefly who lights lanterns in the dark until dawn breaks." "You are a bucket who catches falling eggs until three smash." "You are a lighthouse who sweeps a beam to guide ships until a ship crashes." A stronger version (optional) If you want more, add the feeling and the constraint: A [one-button] game where you are a [firefly] who [lights lanterns] until [dawn] — it should feel [peaceful but tense]. The test Read your sentence to another team. If they can picture the game and roughly how to play it, you're ready to build. If they ask "wait, what do you actually do?", your verb is missing — fix that first. Approval = scope check An instructor has to approve your pitch before you build. They're checking one thing: can you finish this by Friday with Day 1–2 skills? If not, they'll help you shrink it. That's a good thing.

🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 3 - Design Day Play your game on paper before you build it in Godot. It takes 20 minutes and saves you from building the wrong thing. This is not optional on Day 3. Why bother? Code is slow to change; paper is instant. On paper you find out in 5 minutes whether your idea is fun or confusing — before you spend two days coding it. If it's boring as paper, it'll be boring as code. How to do it (15–20 min) 1. Draw the screen. A big rectangle = your game screen. Sketch where the player starts and where things appear. 2. Make the pieces. Tear paper scraps or use coins/erasers for the player, enemies, coins, goal. 3. Be the computer. One teammate "runs" the game by moving the pieces. Another is the player and says their moves out loud: "I press right... now I jump." 4. Play 30 seconds of it. Walk through a real round: starting, the core loop, and how it ends (Tiny Game Design). 5. Hand it to another team. Let them "play" it. Watch where they get confused — that's a real design problem you just caught for free. What you're looking for Is the core loop actually fun, or just an idea? (Tiny Game Design) Is it clear what to do without explaining? Is it too big? If your paper round takes 10 minutes, your game is too big (The Tiny Game Rules). Then write it down Turn what worked into a short build list — that becomes your MVP Checklist on Day 4. List the pieces you need: player, one enemy, score, win/lose. Don't fall in love with paper The prototype is disposable. Its only job is to answer "is this fun and clear?" Once you know, recycle it and open Godot.

h: The golden rule: don't help, don't explain
How to run a playtest (Day 4 exchange)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 2 - Make It Yours, Day 4 - Production Day Watching someone else play your game is the fastest way to make it better. They'll get stuck in ways you can't see, because you already know how it works. The golden rule: don't help, don't explain When someone plays your game, stay quiet. Don't say "oh you press space" or "no, go left." Their confusion is the data. If they're lost, that's a thing to fix — not a thing to explain away. Write down where they struggle. How to run a playtest (Day 4 exchange) 1. Swap machines with another team. Each plays the other's game for 10 minutes. 2. The makers watch silently and take notes: Where did they pause? What did they try that didn't work? Did they understand the goal? 3. Afterward, the players give feedback in this format: 2 things that work · 1 thing that's confusing · 1 suggestion Giving good feedback Be specific: "I didn't know I could jump" beats "it's confusing." Talk about the game, not the people: "the goal wasn't clear," not "you did this wrong." Lead with what works — it tells the team what to protect. Receiving feedback (don't get defensive) You don't have to act on every note. Collect them all, then decide. Sort feedback into three piles: fix now, fix if time, cut/ignore. If two different testers hit the same problem, that's real — prioritize it. Day 2 version (lighter) In the remix carousel, just leave one sticky note per game: ⭐ something you liked + ❓ one question. Same spirit, faster. Playtest Lead's job The Playtest Lead keeps the running bug list all week and runs the team's side of the exchange. By Friday that list becomes the polish to-do (Day 5 - Polish and Showcase).

h: The method: one main computer + bring pieces in
Back up every day (do not skip)
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day How a team of 3–4 works on one Godot project without GitHub. Decide your method on Day 3 before you start building. The method: one main computer + bring pieces in GitHub is powerful but too heavy for one week (accounts, setup, merge conflicts). Instead: 1. Pick one "main" computer. The Godot project lives here, and the Engineer builds in it. This is the source of truth. 2. Everyone else makes pieces on their own machines — art, sounds, a sketched scene, a bit of script in a text file. 3. Bring pieces to the main computer via a shared drive / USB / cloud folder, and the Engineer drops them into the project. This avoids two people editing the same file and overwriting each other. Adding pieces to the project Art & sound: copy the image/audio file into the project's folder (or drag it into the FileSystem dock). Asset Resources A whole scene someone built: copy their and any files it uses into the project, then instance it (Scenes and Nodes). A bit of code: paste it into the right script on the main computer (don't email whole files around — copy the snippet). Back up every day (do not skip) At the end of each day, copy the entire project folder to a USB or cloud drive. The project folder contains everything. Losing it the night before the showcase is the worst-case scenario. A Godot project = one folder with a file inside. Copy the whole folder, not just one file. Working in parallel without collisions Role | Works on | Where | Engineer | the actual project | main computer | Artist/Sound | art & audio files | their machine → transfer | Playtest Lead | bug list, testing builds | their machine | Producer | checklist, helping | floats | Then merge pieces onto the main computer. See Team Roles. Name your files clearly , , . "Untitled (3).png" helps no one. Future-you on Friday will be grateful.

🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 3 - Design Day, Day 4 - Production Day · 🖨️ Print one card per team. Everyone on the team has a real job so no one just watches. Roles can rotate day to day — try to make sure each person both codes and does something else during the week. The four roles (teams of 3–4) 🎬 Producer / Lead Keeps the team on track. Holds the MVP Checklist, watches the clock, and protects scope (The Tiny Game Rules). Speaks at stand-up. Not the boss — the person who keeps everyone unblocked. 💻 Engineer (1–2 people) Owns the scripts and scenes. Wires up movement, collisions, spawning, screens. On a team of 4, two engineers split features (e.g. "you do the player, I do the enemies"). 🎨 Artist / Sound Owns how the game looks and sounds. Finds or makes sprites and audio (Asset Resources, AudioStreamPlayer), picks the color palette, makes the title screen look good. Uses variables to tune feel without deep code (GDScript Basics). 🧪 Playtest Lead Owns quality. Runs the game constantly, keeps a written bug list, leads the Day 4 playtest exchange, and decides (with the Producer) what's a fix vs. a cut. How: Playtesting. Working at the same time Only one person edits the main project at a time (see Sharing Files on a Team). So split work that doesn't collide: Engineer builds in the project on the main computer. Artist makes/collects art and sound on another machine. Playtest Lead writes the bug list and tests builds. Producer updates the checklist and helps wherever it's thin. Then bring the pieces together on the main computer. Mixed experience levels First-timers shine as Artist/Sound or Playtest Lead and still write some code. Put a confident Day-2 coder in the Engineer seat. Everyone codes something during the week.

🏠 Curriculum Map · 🖨️ Print this and post it on the wall. A tiny game is a short game with tight constraints, made fast, built around a single idea. That's the whole camp. These three rules keep you out of trouble: 1. One core idea If you can't say what your game is in one sentence, it's too big. Cut until you can. (See One-Sentence Pitch.) 2. Playable in under 3 minutes A whole play — start to win-or-lose — should fit in about 3 minutes. Short games get finished and get played. 3. Done is better than perfect Cut features, not deadlines. A small game that works beats a big game that's broken. Every time. The mantra One idea. Three minutes. Done beats perfect. These come from the spirit of CU Boulder's Tiny Game Studio — fluency through constraints. Constraints aren't a limitation here; they're the point.

h: Constraints make design easier, not harder
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · Used on Day 3 - Design Day The crash course in designing a game small enough to finish this week. Read with The Tiny Game Rules. Start with the core loop The core loop is what the player does over and over, every few seconds. Name it before anything else: Pac-Man: move, eat dots, avoid ghosts. Flappy Bird: tap, don't hit a pipe. A coin game: move, grab coins, dodge the bad thing. If you can't describe what the player does every 5 seconds, you don't have a game yet — you have a setting. Find the verb. Constraints make design easier, not harder A blank page is the enemy. Limits give you something to push against. That's why every game this week takes a constraint: One screen — no scrolling One mechanic — the player really does one thing One button — the whole game is one key Pick one. It instantly tells you what your game is not, which is most of the work. Scope: your idea ÷ 4 Whatever you first imagine, it's about 4× too big for the time you have. Cut it down: 10 levels → 1 level (or endless) A story → a situation 5 enemy types → 1 enemy, maybe 2 Multiplayer → single player You can always add back if you have time. You can't add back time. Find the fun fast Build the core loop first and play it Day 3–4. If grabbing the coin isn't fun with a gray box, no amount of art will save it. If it is fun as boxes, art makes it shine. Prototype before you polish (Paper Prototyping). Juice (save for last) "Juice" = the small feedback that makes actions feel good: a sound on pickup, a little screen shake, the score popping. It's powerful but it's Day 5 polish, never a Day 3–4 priority (Day 5 - Polish and Showcase). A good tiny-game idea fits this template "It's a game where you [one verb] to [one goal] while [one obstacle], and it ends when [one condition]." If yours fits, you're ready. → One-Sentence Pitch

h: How to use a downloaded asset
b: 🏠 Curriculum Map · Used all week, especially Day 2 - Make It Yours and Day 4 - Production Day Free art, sound, and music you're allowed to use. Check the license — these are all free for projects like ours, but always read the "license" note on a page before using it. 🎨 Art (sprites, backgrounds, icons) Kenney.nl — huge packs of clean game art, totally free, no attribution required. Best first stop. OpenGameArt.org — big community library (check each item's license). itch.io game assets — tons of free sprite packs. Piskel — free in-browser tool to draw your own pixel art sprites and animations. 🔊 Sound effects jsfxr — click a preset (coin, jump, hit, powerup), get a retro sound instantly, download . (AudioStreamPlayer) ChipTone — more control, same idea, in-browser. Freesound.org — recorded sounds (account needed; check licenses). 🎵 Music Kenney music packs — free loops, no attribution. Incompetech — Kevin MacLeod's royalty-free music (attribution required — credit him). BeepBox — make your own chiptune music loop in the browser, free. How to use a downloaded asset 1. Download the file ( for art, / for sound, for music). 2. Drag it into your project's FileSystem dock in Godot. 3. Art → set it as a Sprite's texture. Sound → set it as an AudioStreamPlayer's stream (AudioStreamPlayer). 4. On a team, route asset files through your main computer. Make a few of your own Even one self-drawn sprite (Piskel) or one self-made sound (jsfxr) makes a game feel personal. Mix found + made. Licenses matter "Free" can still mean "credit the author." If a page says attribution is required (like Incompetech), put the author's name on your title or credits screen. When in doubt, use Kenney — no attribution needed.

🏠 Curriculum Map · Every term in one place. Skim it Day 1; come back when a word is fuzzy. Godot & engine terms Node — one building block that does one job (show a picture, play a sound). Scenes and Nodes Scene — a tree of nodes saved together as a file. Can be reused inside other scenes. Scenes and Nodes Instance / Instancing — a copy of a scene placed into the game. Build one Enemy scene, spawn 50 instances. Spawning and Timers Root node — the top node of a scene; everything else hangs under it. Inspector — the right-side panel showing the selected node's properties. Godot Editor Tour Main scene — the screen that loads first when the game runs. Godot Editor Tour — "from the project's root folder," used in file paths. Scene Switching Code terms (GDScript) GDScript — Godot's Python-like coding language. GDScript Basics Variable — a named container for a value ( ). GDScript Basics Function — a named block of code you can run ( ). GDScript Basics — marks a variable so it shows in the Inspector for easy tweaking. GDScript Basics — runs once when a node enters the game. GDScript Basics — runs every frame (60×/sec). = time since last frame. GDScript Basics — like but at a steady rate; use it for movement. Movement and Input Vector2 — a pair of numbers : a position or direction on screen. Movement and Input — deletes a node from the game (use for grabbed coins, dead enemies). Area2D — red text in the Output panel when code can't run. Read the first line; it usually names the line number. Godot Editor Tour Node types you'll use — a thing that moves and bumps into stuff (the player). Movement and Input — detects overlaps (hits, pickups). Needs a CollisionShape2D. Area2D — defines the shape an Area2D detects. No shape = detects nothing. Area2D — waits, then fires a signal. Spawning and Timers — shows text on screen (score, messages). Score and UI — keeps UI pinned to the screen instead of moving with the world. Score and UI — plays a sound or music. AudioStreamPlayer Signal — a node's announcement that something happened ("doorbell"); other nodes connect and react. Signals Design & process terms Tiny game — a short game with tight constraints, built fast around one idea. The Tiny Game Rules Core loop — what the player does over and over, every few seconds. Tiny Game Design Constraint — a rule you design within (one screen, one button). Sparks ideas. Constraint Cards Scope — how big your game is. Too much scope = unfinished. "Idea ÷ 4." Tiny Game Design Prototype — a rough, fast version (even on paper) to test if it's fun. Paper Prototyping MVP — Minimum Viable Product: the smallest playable version. MVP Checklist Playtest — watching someone play to find problems. Playtesting Juice — small feedback (shake, sound, pop) that makes a game feel good. Polish only. Tiny Game Design Feature freeze — the point where you stop adding and only fix/polish. Day 5 - Polish and Showcase Export / Build — turning your project into something others can play. Exporting Your Game

🏠 Curriculum Map A menu of short breaks to pull from when the room needs an energy shift. Every entry is roughly 10–20 minutes and needs nothing beyond what's already in the room. The half-day camp has two built-in coffee breaks and doesn't require any of these. Use them when Open Studio runs long, when a group is fried after pitch approval on Day 3 - Design Day, or if you ever run the camp as a full day. Nothing here is scheduled — it's a list to reach for, not a plan to follow. Play + Debrief Play something together, then spend a few minutes writing or talking about it. Closest thing to "curriculum" in this list — same "what's the one idea?" muscle from Days 1–3, exercised on something other than Godot. Play a round of a card game (Uno, Spoons, Skip-Bo, whatever someone brought) → one sentence each: "what was the one rule that made this fun or frustrating?" Watch a 2-minute gameplay clip of something the group likes → discuss the player's one action and the one tension Classic playground game (tag variant, Ninja, Rock-Paper-Scissors tournament) → debrief what rule made it interesting instead of just chaos Trade "best game I played this year" stories in pairs, then each pair reports one out to the group Play a physical/tabletop version of a video game genre (a maze on paper, a stacking game, a matching game) → tie back to "action + tension + failure state" (Tiny Game Design) Mafia / Werewolf (great for a bigger group, needs one confident narrator) Charades, but only game titles or game characters "Guess the mechanic" — describe a game's one rule without naming it, others guess the game Screen-Free Design Games Little design-thinking exercises that don't touch a computer — good energy shift without derailing from the week's actual skills. Design a game using only what's in your pocket/backpack as pieces — 10 minutes, then pitch it in one sentence (One-Sentence Pitch) "Yes, and" game design — one person proposes a rule, the next adds one more, see how far a game idea can go before it collapses Redesign a classic game with one twist ("Tag, but you're all it," "Tic-tac-toe on a bigger board") — playtest it right there Draw a title screen for a game that doesn't exist yet, based on a random word prompt Constraint speed-round: draw a card from Constraint Cards just for fun, 3-minute pitch, no building required Build a tower/structure from cups or cards with a rule twist each round (classic team-builder, easy design-thinking bridge) Outside / Active No debrief needed — the point is leaving the screen and the chairs. Free time outside, no agenda Short walk around the building Gaga ball, kickball, four square, capture the flag, or whatever the outdoor space supports Water balloon or water gun break on a hot day Relay races, sack races, three-legged races Frisbee or a simple catch game Scavenger hunt (nature items, or themed objects) Obstacle course using whatever's on hand (cones, hula hoops, jump ropes) Student-led stretch or warmup (rotate who leads it) Quiet / Reflective For after a heavy stretch — post-lunch, post-pitch-approval, end of day — when the room needs to come down, not up. Journaling prompt: "What's one thing about your game that surprised you today?" Quick sketch break: your character, your title screen, or just doodle Silent reading (bring-a-book day) "One good thing, one hard thing" — everyone writes both, sharing optional Draw your game's world/setting even if it never shows up on screen Write a fake review of your own game, like a store page blurb Team / Social / Icebreakers Good right after a break, or whenever the room's energy is scattered. Two Truths and a Lie (game-themed) Team name / mascot brainstorm for whoever hasn't picked one (Team Roles) Trivia round: guess the game from its one mechanic described out loud Human bingo card themed around games people have played "Would you rather" — game edition (would you rather your game had no sound or no color?) Compliment circle — one specific thing you liked about a teammate's work this week Speed-friending: 2 minutes per pair, then rotate

🏠 Curriculum Map · Hand out at the showcase · 🖨️ Print as a take-home. You made games this week. Here's how to keep making them after camp. It's all free. Keep Godot Godot is free forever — download it at godotengine.org on any computer (Windows, Mac, Linux). Bring your camp project home on a USB or upload it (see Exporting Your Game). Learn more (free tutorials) Official Godot docs & tutorials — docs.godotengine.org. Start again with "Your first 2D game," then try "Your first 3D game." GDQuest — gdquest.com and their YouTube — excellent beginner-to-intermediate Godot lessons. Brackeys (YouTube) — friendly, popular Godot tutorial series. 20 Games Challenge — 20gameschallenge — a list of classic games to rebuild in order, each one teaching new skills. Perfect next step from tiny games. Make more tiny games Game jams — short events (a weekend to a week) where everyone makes a game on a theme. Browse itch.io/jams. Look for beginner-friendly or "no theme" jams. Mini Jam / Ludum Dare / GMTK Game Jam — well-known recurring jams (some have age guidance — check, and do them with a parent). Keep using constraints — give yourself "one button, one screen, one hour" and just go. Share what you make Upload to itch.io (free) so friends and family can play in a browser (Exporting Your Game). The habit that matters most Finish small things. A pile of ten tiny finished games will teach you more than one giant game you never complete. That's the whole philosophy of this camp — The Tiny Game Rules. Next weekend challenge Pick a constraint, set a 2-hour timer, and make one tiny game start to finish. Show someone. Repeat.

h: Day 3 (Wed) — Design Day: Pitch, Teams, Prototype
b: A 5-day game development camp modeled on CU Boulder's Tiny Game Studio (ATLS 4060) philosophy: tiny games — short games with tight technical constraints, built quickly, around a single idea. Instead of Bitsy/PuzzleScript/Pico-8, campers use one engine (Godot 4) and progress from guided template games to a fully original team game presented on the final day. Structure: Each day = Teaching Block (3 hrs, required) + Open Studio (optional work time) Team size: 3–4 per team This is the overview. The full lesson-by-lesson curriculum, student references, and instructor notes live in the Curriculum Map. Camp Goals By Friday, every camper can: 1. Navigate Godot: scenes, nodes, the editor, running a game 2. Read and modify GDScript (variables, signals, , simple conditionals) 3. Build 1–3 tiny games from tutorials/templates 4. Design within constraints: scope a game idea down to one mechanic 5. Ship one original team game and present it at the Friday Arcade Showcase The Tiny Game Rules (post these on the wall all week): One core idea. If you can't say it in one sentence, it's too big. Playable in under 3 minutes. Done is better than perfect. Cut features, not deadlines. Week at a Glance Day | Theme | Output | --- | --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | Mon | Meet Godot — build Game #1 from a tutorial | Dodge the Creeps (everyone) | Tue | Make it yours — remix Game #1 into Game #2 | Personal remix | Wed | Design day — pitch, form teams, prototype | Team pitch + paper prototype + project setup | Thu | Production day — build the team game | Playable MVP | Fri | Polish + Arcade Showcase (4–6 PM for parents) | Final game + presentation | Games #1 and #2 are individual/pair skill-builders. Game #3 is the original team game. (Fast campers may squeeze in an extra micro-game during Open Studio — that's the "1–3 games" range.) Day 1 (Mon) — Meet Godot 📓 Full lesson + student reference: Day 1 - Meet Godot 🖨️ Print before camp: Day 1 Student Checklist (one per student) Goal: Everyone leaves with a complete, running game they typed themselves — Dodge the Creeps in Godot 4. Teaching Block Schedule Time | Block | 9:00–9:15 | Welcome + What is a Tiny Game? | 9:15–9:40 | Godot Editor Tour + Project Setup | 9:40–10:20 | Part 1: Build the Player (nodes, animations, script) | 10:20–10:30 | ☕ Break | 10:30–11:00 | Part 2: Build the Mob (enemy scene) | 11:00–11:10 | ☕ Break | 11:10–11:45 | Part 3: Main Scene (wire everything together) | 11:45–12:00 | Stand-up close + exit ticket | This is our own Godot 4 walkthrough — not the official docs video (which uses Godot 3). See Asset Resources for the inspiration video link. What students are building Dodge the Creeps: a character you move with arrow keys, enemies that fly in from the edges, survive as long as you can. It covers: scenes, nodes, AnimatedSprite2D, GDScript, movement, signals, collision, and spawning with timers. Open Studio (optional) HUD (score + start button), background color, background music, death sound, stretch goals. See the Stretch Goals section in Day 1 - Meet Godot. Day 2 (Tue) — Make It Yours (Remix) 📓 Full lesson + student reference: Day 2 - Make It Yours Goal: Move from following code to changing code. Game #2 = a personal remix of Game #1. Teaching Block 0:00–0:15 — Warm-up: read the code Project a chunk of yesterday's player script. Ask: "What happens if I change this number? Delete this line?" Change it live. Normalize breaking things. 0:15–0:45 — Mini-lessons (pick 3, 10 min each) Swapping sprites and sounds (importing assets, AnimatedSprite2D) Variables as game-feel dials: speed, spawn rate, scale Adding a new rule with (e.g., touching a star = +10 points) Timers and signals (e.g., speed up every 10 seconds) 0:45–2:30 — Remix sprint Each camper (or pair) remixes Dodge the Creeps into a new game. Require at least 3 changes across 2 categories: Look/sound: new art, new audio, new title Rules: new pickup, lives, win condition, second enemy behavior Feel: speed, gravity, spawn rates, screen size Remix prompts for the stuck: "the player is a fish," "dodging is collecting," "the game speeds up forever," "two-button game only." 2:30–3:00 — Playtest carousel Rotate seats every 3 minutes, play each other's remixes, leave one sticky note: Something you liked + One question. Open Studio (optional) Keep remixing, or start the optional micro-game challenge: a one-screen, one-button game from scratch (this is the path to "3 games"). Day 3 (Wed) — Design Day: Pitch, Teams, Prototype 📓 Full lesson + student reference: Day 3 - Design Day Goal: Shift from learning the engine to making something original. Leave with teams, a locked one-sentence pitch, a paper prototype, and an empty-but-set-up Godot project. Teaching Block 0:00–0:30 — Tiny game design crash course Core loop ("what does the player do every 5 seconds?"), constraints breed creativity, scope ("your idea ÷ 4"). Show examples of jam games made in 48 hours. 0:30–1:00 — Brainstorm with constraints Roll the constraint dice (or draw cards). Every game must satisfy the camp constraint set: One screen OR one mechanic OR one button (pick at least one) Playable in under 3 minutes Buildable with skills from Days 1–2 (movement, collision, pickups, score, timers) Solo silent brainstorm (8 min, sticky notes) → cluster ideas on the wall → dot-vote. 1:00–1:30 — Form teams + pitch Teams of 3–4 form around the top ideas. Each team writes its one-sentence pitch ("You are a who until ") and gets it approved by an instructor. Instructor's job here: cut scope ruthlessly. 1:30–2:15 — Paper prototype Draw the screen, the player, the obstacles. Walk through 30 seconds of play out loud. Another team plays the paper version and asks questions. 2:15–3:00 — Project setup + roles Create the team Godot project, build the main scene skeleton, get a player moving on screen before the block ends. Assign rotating roles: Lead/Producer — keeps the task list, watches scope Engineer(s) — scripts and scenes Artist/Sound — sprites, palette, audio (Kenney, jsfxr/BeepBox) Playtest lead — runs tests, logs bugs Sharing work on one project: simplest is one "main" computer + others build pieces (scenes, art, sounds) and transfer via Google Drive. I thought about using GitHub but its too complicated for this and everyone would need an account or we would have to have all this setup before hand. Open Studio (optional) Start building. Teams that move fast: get the core mechanic playable today. Day 4 (Thu) — Production Day 📓 Full lesson + student reference: Day 4 - Production Day Goal: A playable Minimal Viable Project (MVP) by end of teaching block. Ugly is fine; playable is "mandatory". Teaching Block 0:00–0:10 — Stand-up Each team, 60 seconds: done yesterday / doing today / what's blocking us. 0:10–0:20 — MVP talk Define MVP: player can play, win or lose, and restart. That's it. Everything else is polish. Have each team write their MVP checklist on an index card; tape it to the monitor. 0:20–2:20 — Build sprint Instructors float and unblock. Run on-demand micro-lessons at a side table as needs emerge (typical requests: scene switching for a title/game-over screen, score labels, restart button, background music, simple enemy AI). 2:20–2:50 — Mandatory playtest exchange Teams swap machines and play each other's MVPs for 10 minutes, then deliver: 2 things that work, 1 confusing thing, 1 suggestion. Teams triage feedback into fix tomorrow vs. cut. 2:50–3:00 — Scope check Each team crosses off anything on their list they won't finish by tomorrow's 3 PM build deadline. Instructor signs off. Open Studio (optional) This is the high-value work session — expect most teams to stay. Hard rule: no new features after today. Tomorrow is polish only. Day 5 (Fri) — Polish + Arcade Showcase 📓 Full lesson + student reference: Day 5 - Polish and Showcase Goal: Finish, present, celebrate. Showcase is 4:00–6:00 PM so parents can attend after work (adjust as needed) — which makes Friday the one day where Open Studio time is effectively part of the schedule. Teaching Block (morning) 0:00–0:10 — Stand-up + freeze warning Feature freeze is already in effect. Today: bug fixes, title screen, sounds, juice (screen shake, particles — only if stable). 0:10–2:00 — Polish sprint Must-haves before the showcase: title screen with the game's name and team names, a way to restart, no crashes in 3 minutes of play. 2:00–2:30 — Presentation prep Each team preps a 3–4 minute presentation: game name + one-sentence pitch, live demo (a teammate plays while another talks), one thing that was hard and how they solved it, one thing they'd add with another week. 2:30–3:00 — Dress rehearsal Each team runs its presentation once for the room. Fix timing, decide who talks/who plays. Afternoon (before doors open) Final bug fixes only — no new anything 3:00 — hard deadline: working builds on the demo machine(s) (export or run-from-editor) 3:00–4:00: set up arcade stations (team game + Day 2 remixes), voting tickets, certificates; teams take a break 🕹️ Arcade Showcase — 4:00–6:00 PM 4:00–4:15 — Doors open, parents arrive, games on attract-mode at stations 4:15–5:00 — Team presentations (3–4 min each + applause) 5:00–5:45 — Open arcade: all games playable at stations, parents and campers vote with tickets for superlatives — Most Creative, Best Feel, Funniest, Best Title Screen. Every team wins something. 5:45–6:00 — Awards, certificates, where to keep going (Godot docs, GDQuest, 20 Games Challenge, itch.io game jams), and how to take projects home (USB/email/itch.io upload)

When someone gets stuck on "how do I make it move again?", they open Movement and Input instead of asking you to rewind the video.
